speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is of course desirable to reduce in every possible way the very great expenditure which is necessitated by the war, and I have asked the various heads of branches in the Department of Militia and Defence for a report upon that subject. The major part of the expenditure naturally consists of the pay and subsistence of the men, and the provision of uniforms and equipment and stores of various kinds which are necessary for the purposes of the war. So far as. these are concerned, and they form the vhstly greater part of the expenditure, we could not expect to reduce the expenditure very much, but there may be some minor matters in respect of which reductions can be accomplished. If there is any such possibility we shall not fail to avail ourselves of it.
With regard to recruiting, representations have been made to us from various quarters urging the necessity of some further system. We have received a delegation which very strongly pressed upon the Government the necessity of a complete registration of the manhood of Canada, and eventually of conscription.' We have not had an opportunity of giving adequate consideration to this proposal, but the Department of (Militia and Defence has endeavoured, particularly during the past six or nine months, so to guide recruiting that the agricultural, commercial and industrial strength of Canada shall not be unduly weakened. It is, of

me,

course, impossible for a country like Canada to raise 310,000 men without any inconvenience to the various industries, such as agriculture, manufacturing, and the various commercial activities of the country, but we have endeavoured to arrange with recruiting officers that where a very large number of men have been taken from a district which is a centre of a particular industry of importance to the country, recruiting in that particular place shall be _so directed that the industry in question shall not be unduly hampered. So far as agriculture is concerned, a general order was passed by the Department of Militia giving permission to the men enlisted in all parts of Canada to engage in agriculture during a certain period this spring, to assist in ploughing and seeding. Representations were made to us, on behalf of some agricultural interests, that in some parts of the country this permission was not being availed of to a very large extent. So, upon my suggestion to the Deputy Minister of Militia, an instruction was sent out to the officers commanding the various battalions directing them to encourage and even to urge the men to assist in this work, which is of the highest possible importance, as we all agree that agricultural production should, during this war, as indeed at all
5 p.m. times, be brought up to its highest limit. We have endeavoured to relieve the situation, so far as possible, by such means.
I have detained the com'mittee at very considerable length, but I think not without some advantage, in making members of the House acquainted with the very great magnitude of the work which is being carried on and with the very valuable services which have been rendered to this country by the officers of the Department of Militia and Defence. I have found them inspired throughout by a splendid spirit of earnestness and devotion to the public interest. It is almost impossible for hon. members of this House who have not been brought closely in touch with the activities of the department, to realize the enormous burdens of responsibility and of work which have been undertaken by the officers of the department, which have been assumed by them without a murmur or complaint, and which have been carried out, I believe, in a manner which reflects credit not only upon them but upon the administration of public affairs in this country. In common with all the people of this country, they

have been called upon for a certain sacrifice, and they have made that sacrifice cheerfully and patriotically.
The spirit of our people has been so splendid that no words of mine are needed in commendation of it. Who would have imagined, in August, 1914, that in less than [DOT] 18 months more than 300,000 men in Canada would have flocked to the colours? The difficulty has been not ' to obtain enlistments, but to prbvide uniforms, equipment, arms, and all the necessaries for war. But more than that, we in Canada, in common with all the citizens of the Empire, can congratulate ourselves upon the splendid courage and endurance which our men have displayed at the front. It was a supreme test to which they were subjected. They -had not been trained to arms as had the forces of the enemy whom they went to encounter. Eew of them had had any military training before the outbreak of war. They went to the front and they met the very best troops that 'Europe could produce. They met the forces of the enemy, in the first instance, under the most trying conditions that could be imagined.
It would be impossible, I believe, for any man now within the sound of my voice to realize the test to which the Canadian troops were subjected on the 22nd April, 1915. I have said before that only those who have seen in the hospitals, men still suffering, months afterwards, from the effects of that gas attack, could realize what it meant to the Canadian forces who were subjected to it. They not only endured that, they remained in the *'trenches and held them, held them not only in the face of that attack, but in the face of overwhelming numbers, and they did not retire, not a man of them, until they received orders to do so, and some of them did not retire even then. To-day the men at the front, unless I am misinformed, are holding one of the most important and perilous portions of the line in France or in Belgium. We can rest assured, from the spirit which was shown a year ago, that the Canadian troops who hold that line will hold it to the end, and, while we mourn the casualties which bring sorrow to so many homes, we know that in the outcome the Canadian troops at the front can be relied upon to do their duty. We are all conscious of the -sacrifice which this struggle for liberty and the preservation of our institutions demands, and although Canada is conscious, from the Atlantic to

the Pacific, of that tremendous sacrifice of life and of resources, she faces the future with undaunted eye and with a firm heart.

I desire to ask the Prime Minister a few questions for information, as I did not wish to interrupt him in the course of his remarks. I am sure that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will cordially endorse the appreciation, just delivered by the Prime Minister, of the Canadian forces. I quite agree with the right hon. gentleman when he stated that considering the fact that our soldiers were inexperienced in the art of war they have accomplished great deeds, and have reflected great credit upon our country. I am sure that Canadians all look forward to a continuance, during the balance of the war, of the same courage and distinction on the part of the Canadian troops as we have witnessed in the past.
The right hon. gentleman has given ue a very great deal of information this afternoon, which I am sure the House will receive with pleasure, and which will be valuable to the country. I quite appreciate the fact also, that the Department of Militia had very suddenly thrust upon at a vast amount of labour, and I agree with the Prime Minister in saying that a great deal of credit is due to that branch of the public service for its splendid work during the past 18 months or more. Sometimes, however, I feel that there has been such an amount of extra work pressed upon that particular department that possibly there has been, in regard to details, a lack of organization, that has not been to the advantage of the country. I was,glad to hear the Prime Minister state that he had asked the various heads of the branches of the Militia Department for a statement showing where, if possible, they could minimize expenditures on the war credit vote. I think that this matter might very well engage the serious consideration of the Government. I do not think that the country would be too critical as to small details of war expenditure, but, in the main, they will expect from the Government an oversight and direction in respect to war expenditures that will make them feel that their interests are being protected.
As was pointed out last year, a special responsibility rests upon the Government, as a body, in respect to war expenditures that does not attach to them in connection with expenditures by departments. In
205*
the latter case, ministers come to Parliament and designate in the Supply Bill the various detailed amounts which they ask Parliament to vote, but in the case of the resolution before the committee, a flat vote of $250,000,000 is asked for as a war credit vote. There are no details given, Parliament surrenders to the Government its control over the expenditure, and expects it to exercise that oversight as to detail which Parliaments usually exercise in respect to supply votes to the various departments of Government. The expenditures made by the Militia Department, or by any depart-iment, in connection with the war, are therefore under the responsibility of the Government as a body, and that responsibility does not rest upon any one particular minister, or upon 'any one particular department. Last session of Parliament, on the occasion of the consideration of a resolution similar to this, I gave to the commit-,tee a statement, or a minute of council of the Lords of the Treasury in England as to the system that should be followed .in respect to war expenditures, and I would like to know from the Prime Minister whether that system is followed rigidly, as we were promised laet year. The principle there laid down is that in the absence of estimates, or details of general war expenditure, each department should furnish to the Treasury Board, or to the Government, a detailed statement of probable expenditure during the forthcoming year, and that no expenditures should be made by any department without the authorization by Order in Council of the Treasury Board or of the Government. I should like to have some information from the Prime Minister as to whether that system is followed. Further, under the terms of the minute of the British Treasury Board, it was ordained that, not only the war credit vote, but the ordinary war and naval credits also should be expended in that manner. The reason is obvious. It is almost impossible to distinguish between expenditures made by the Militia Department, or the Naval Department, as to what are ordinary, or peace, expenditures, and what are war expenditures. I would say that all expenditures made by the Naval branch have reference, in some degree or other, to the war. Therefore, I think it would be a very wise course for the Government in the future, if it has not done so in the past, to insist that these ordinary militia and naval expenditures be authorized by the Government, or by a committee of the Govern-

ment, or by some proper authority, whatever that may be. I do not wish to elaborate this point as rl discussed it fully last year. 'I think we had the assurance of the Government that it would not shirk its responsibility in respect to the oversight of all war expenditures and that nothing should be left to the entire initiative of any department. It is true that war expenditures must be initiated by. some department, but before the authorization is made they should be considered by the Government, and before any expenditure is actually made, it should be seen that the authorization has also been duly made. I said that there is a distinction between a credit vote and the ordinary parliamentary vote in the form of the Supply Bill. Inasmuch as Parliament surrenders its control absolutely over the $250,000,000 that is to be voted by this resolution, it is only fair that Parliament should receive all possible information from the Government before the resolution is passed.
It is needless for me to say that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will unhesitatingly vote the amount asked for by this resolution and accelerate its passing. We are as much interested in it as are the members of the Government and therefore I venture the suggestion, and the request, that the committee should be furnished with a statement showing the probable nature of the expenditures to be made out of the amount mentioned in the resolution. At page 49 of the printed memorandum, No. 2, which has been placed before Parliament, I find a detailed statement of the expenditures since the beginning of the war down to December 31, 1915. I think it would be well if the Prime Minister would submit to the committee a statement on that basis showing the' particulars, as far as they can be obtained, of the proposed war expenditure of this year. I think that not only the Militia Department should furnish this information to the Government to transmit to Parliament but that the other departments ought to do the same thing. I should like to say, because it is possible I omitted to do so before, that other departments, such as the Department of Justice and the Department of Trade and Commerce, which are expending war moneys should also have from the Government an authorization before engaging in any expenditure. I also think that they, as well as the Department of Militia and Defence should, as far as they can, furnish us with particulars of the expenditures

which they propose to make during the year.
That is all I have to say in a general way regarding these expenditures. There are a few questions I should like to ask the Prime Minister, and the information can be given later in the day. I, of course, wish to reiterate, in case I have not already made myself clear, that the committee should be furnished by the minister with a statement showing the particulars of the proposed expenditure for this year. There is one matter upon which I should like some information and that is the operations of the War Purchasing Commission. I understand that that body makes pretty nearly; all the purchases required for |he Department of Militia and Defence in connection with the war. I would like to know if in all cases the system of tender and contract is carried out by that body. I understood the right hon. gentleman to say this afternoon that such was the practice. Before the Public Accounts Committee a few weeks ago a statement was made by the Director of Contracts that there was a patronage list in connection with purchases made by that commission. I was somewhat astounded to hear that statement, because I had hoped that such was not the condition of affairs. If there is an occasion when we should be delivered from a system of patronage it is in connection with the spending of public money for the prosecution of the war. If it is true, as stated by the Director of Contracts, that a patronage list exists in the Militia Department, and is used by the War Purchasing Commission, then I say that such condition should not exiist and that such .patronage list should be immediately abolished. The public should have that assurance from the Government. I may be making an argument that may be very easily answered, because I rather gather from the expression of the right hon. gentleman who leads the Government that he is under the impression that my remarks are hardly apropos, because the Purchasing Commission does not use a patronage list. However, I should like to have a statement from him as to what is the practice of the commission, because we have the statement of the Director of Contracts that such a list does exist.
Further, statements have been made during the present session by many hon. gentlemen on this side of the House indicating the introduction of partisanship and patronage into war expenditures in some localities in Canada at least. I am sure it was not gratifying to members of Parliament or to

the country to learn of these facts. I do not propose saying anything further upon that point other than to emphasize the fact that if any portion of these war expenditures is made upon the basis of patronage it is absolutely indefensible and the country is entitled to an assurance from the Government who are collectively responsible for the proper expenditure of this amount that no such things did occur in the past and that they shall not occur in the future.
I noticed in the press recently that there was a surplusage of officers in the Canadian Overseas Forces. I have also been informed that the officers training schools throughout Canada are to be suspended very shortly, on May 1st, I think, owing to the fact that we have now more officers than we actually require. 1 am referring to this particularly because, rightly or wrongly, I am under the impression that there is an unnecessary expenditure in this direction. There are in England to-day many Canadian officers who went overseas with their regiments, and there is now apparently no service for them to perform. Again, we have had returned to Canada officers who went overseas but who were discharged, or at all events, returned to Canada, on the ground that they were incompetent or unnecessary in the overseas' forces; and in many cases I believe these officers are still retained by the department and, I suppose, still receive their pay. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say that the Government and Parliament should ma^ke an effort to minimize war expenses as much as possible, for we all realize that our expenses on account of the war are mounting rapidly, and fast assuming such proportions that we shall be faced with a serious financial responsibility in the future. I therefore venture to suggest that a very great saving might possibly be made by the reduction of these officers in the Canadian forces, if they really are not necessary. I would make this further suggestion :	better judgment and discretion
should be exercised in the selection of officers than has been the case in the past. I know that in Canada there have been placed at the head of regiments men who were never militia officers and who had never taken an officer's training course- men who had never evidenced any capacity for leadership, and who, in the judgment of the public who know them, were unfitted for the positions which they held. If there is a surplusage of officers-and that objection should be removed if it does exist-surely we must have some men who have had
either some experience at the front or some militia experience, and I think .these should be given the preference in the selection of officers. I do not make these remarks in any censorious spirit, on the contrary 1 want to pay my tribute to the man who duns the uniform in this great crisis, and who is willing to make the sacrifice of going overseas and doing the very beet he can. I feel that way myself, because it will not be my privilege to offer myself for service in this great war. Notwithstanding my admiration for their self-sacrifice, I have no hesitation in making these observations in respect to officers for the overseas force, particularly if I am correct in believing that a large number of them are unable to perform any service because there is no service for them to perform. I have no hesitation whatever in urging upon the Government, or the department responsible for the selection of the officers commanding regiments that it is proposed to send overseas, that only men who have had some experience or have some natural capacity for the position should be placed in command of regiments.
There is just one other matter to which I wish to refer before taking my seat, and that will be in the nature of a question to the Prime Minister. I should like to know whether war expenditures are submitted in detail to the Government periodically. On page 35 of the printed memorandum No. 2, the monthly expenditures since the beginning of the war are shown. Possibly they have been prepared just recently for the information of Parliament. Is it the practice of the spending departments to submit to the Government monthly statements of their expenses, and an estimate . or requisition giving details of any expenditures they propose to make?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As regards my hon. friend's question relating to the requirements of each departmeent, I have given him a statement of what has been spent during the past year, and I can get the information in detail as to the requirements of the different departments for the coming year. That can be given to the committee, a little later on. As regards patronage lists in connection with the War Puchasing Commission I had never heard of any until my hon. friend mentioned it to-day and I do not believe that any such lists exist. I sent out just now for the chairman of the War Purchasing Commission, but I find that he is not in town.

When he returns I shall ask him to give full information on this subject.
As far as the surplusage of officers is concerned I cabled for some information on this subject a few days ago and I shall be glad to give it to the committee when I receive it The Canadian establishment is, I believe, somewhat different from the British establishment by which our men are governed when they go to the front. Where a regiment in Great Britain becomes practically broken up through the necessity of sending drafts to the front, a surplusage of officers may occur from time to time. As regards officers in Great Britain, I understand from the deputy minister that although there may be a surplusage so far as the regular authorized establishment is concerned, all the officers are employed in someway while in Great Britain. In fact I remember seeing a telegram in response to an inquiry a few days ago, to the effect that there were only two officers in Great Britain who were not attached to some unit there. Although the number may be above the recognized establishment, if the information which I have given just now is correct, all those officers are employed and made useful in some way.
My hon. friend speaks of sending to the iront only officers of experience and capacity. I hope no one thinks that we have enough officers of military experience for these three hundred thousand men.
I intended to make reference entirely to regiments recruiting in Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We do not possess in Canada men of military experience according to the standard my hon. friend has set up. The best we have been able to do is to take men who are inspired by a patriotic desire to serve in this war-some of them have had a little military experience in training camps, perhaps, some of them have had none at all, but they come rorward-and we judge of their cajpaeity best we can. It is absolutely impossible for any man, my hon. friend or any other, to know just to what extent any officer, when he is put in command of a - regiment, or brigade, or division, at the front, is going to develop the qualities of leadership and capacity which are necessary for the command of such units. Men comparatively inexperienced are necessarily sent to the front after such training as may be possible in this country and in Great Britain. It ought to be a source of very great pride to all of us that, with very few

exceptions indeed, the men "who have had to contend with the difficulties arising from inexperience have made good, as they have made good, during the past eighteen months. Some of them have come back through physical unfitness to stand the awful strain imposed upon them at the front. A great many have come back invalided through wounds received or diseases contracted. The men who have come back have been utilized, as far as possible, for the training of units in Canada, so that these units may have the advantage of the knowledge and experience gained by officers who have been at the front.
So far as the war expenditures and the Government's control over those expenditures are concerned, nothing has been paid out of the war appropriations granted by this Parliament-except in the early months of the war as 'to which I gave an explanation last year-that has not . been previously directly authorized by by Order in Council. No department of Government has this appropriation at its command; the appropriation was not so granted by Parliament; it was not granted to any minister, 'but to the Government as a whole. Therefore, a minister, whether the Minister of Militia and Defence, the Minister of Naval Service, or the Minister of Justice-with reference to internment operations-must come to the Government, and the reports of (Council show why payment from the war appropriation is asked and for what purpose. That is done in every case. We have passed thousands of Orders in. Council. of this kind during the past eighteen months. That was not absolutely the case in the first two months of the war. As I explained last year, some payments were made without previous authority of Council by the Department of Militia and Defence. With regard to these payments, we had them all collected and put in a report, which was submitted to the Treasury Board. The Treasury Board spent days upon them and went over them carefully, and finally an Order in Council was passed giving subsequent authority for payments already contracted, and which had to be contracted unless we were disposed to greatly delay the desptch of the first contingent.
The Minister of Justice, for example,-may desire that a further sum of money shall be placed at the disposal of Major General Sir William Otter in respect of internment operations; he submits a statement, not absolutely in

detail, but of a. general character, showing for what purposes the last appropriation has been paid-so much for food, so much for clothing, so much for other things, the money having been paid out under the supervision of Major General Otter-and showing that, from the experience of the past, there will be required for the next three months a certain sum of money. An' Order in Council is passed placing a certain sum at his disposal, and stating in explicit terms that, so far as supplies are concerned, they must be purchased under the War Purchasing Commission, and under the Order in Council establishing that commission. The same is true of the Department of Naval Service, or of the Department of Militia and Defence. I trust I have made myself clear. I shall be glad to answer any other question.	,

In the session of 1914 we in this House, irrespective of party, voted the $50,000,000 asked for the purposes of carrying on Canada's part in the war. In the session of 1915, we voted $100,000,000 just as readily. We are now called upon to vote $250,000,000 and this we intend to vote in just as generous a manner as on the previous occasion. I wish to refer briefly to one or two matters and first to recruiting. I am not able, perhaps, to give any suggestions to the Government that would assist in stimulating recruiting, and possibly fop, that reason the minister may think that I have not much to say, but I have observed one or two things about recruiting the knowledge of which by the House, I think, would do no harm. I am afraid that throughout the part of the country in which I live no system is followed in connection with recruiting. It may be that the Government has found difficulty-no doubt it has-in mapping out a general plan to cover the whole of Canada. Recruiting appears to be left entirely to each community and the city in which I live handles it for that part of the country. We have a recruiting committee and the same plan exists, I suppose, in many other places both in western and eastern Canada. I believe these local committees look after recruiting very well. Another feature that occurred to me is the scattering of recruits in small batches in small towns which I do not think is in the best interests of the recruits. When I was coming down to Ottawa on the Canadian Pacific railway a few days ago, I saw at the divisional points on the north shore
of Lake' Superior, a few recruits at every station. On inquiry I found that these were some of the towns where twenty-five men had been recruited and were stationed. These men cannot possibly get the training they would be given in a larger centre or at some concentration camp. I venture to believe that they should not be scattered in this way, but rather that they should be sent to some place where a large number of them would be collected and.where they would be given the training they ought to have before they cross the Water. In these small places there is not the equipment for efficient training, nor can the Government maintain in every one of these places an efficient training officer who can train two hundred men as easily as he can train twenty-five.
Another question raised in my part of the country is whether or not the recruits taken out are all physically fit. The information I have is only general, and I can not give specific instances, but that information is to the effect that, in* the anxiety of officers to fill up a battalion, a large number of men are being recruited who are not physically fit and who, in the last resort, when they get across the water, or perhaps even before they leave Canada, will have to be rejected.
1 think it is a mistake to take men into a battalion if they are not physically fit, because their places will have to be fillet later, when, nexbaps, it w:il be too late to give the new men the proper training. There is another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister- and I do so with a good deal of hesitancy. I doubt very much whether some of our piilitia officers in certain parts of the country have the Reeling of responsibility, that they should have when put in charge of such a large number of men. The 1,100 men forming a battalion are really wards of their officers; the officers occupy the same position towards them for the time being, at least, as the schoolmaster or teacher in a college does to the boys who are put under his charge. I question very much whether on all occasions the officers do have the sense of responsibility that they ought to have in regard to the men who are put under their charge. I know an instance that occurred in the city of Regina. A young boy named Darraeh enlisted with the 68th battalion there. The boy's home was in the city of Regina; his parents lived there. He was at home over Sunday; on Monday he became ill. Al-

though the distance from the barracks where he was stationed to hi-s father's office was not more than a mile or a mile and a half, no word was sent to the parents. On Tuesday he became worse; on Wednesday he was put in the hospital, and still no word was sent t'o his parents. On Friday, just a few minutes before the boy died, the parents were communicated with by some person in the hospital, but before the father could reach the hospital the boy had died. Naturally the parents in their bereavement, not having been advised of the boy's illness, felt very bitterly towards some of the people in charge of militia matters in the city of Regina, and one cannot blame them very much for feeling the way they did. I mention -this matter largely for the purpose of indicating that the officers on that occasion should have taken some little precaution to advise the parents of the boy's illness. Occurrences of that kind will not stimulate recruiting in any community. Parents will not allow their boys eighteen, nineteen and twenty yeare of age to enlist if they think that* the boys will not get proper care.
I do not know whether the boy got proper medical attendance or not; I assume that he must have got proper medical attendance when he was in the hospital. The point where the military men were apparently at fault-I heard no defence of the matter at all-was that no communication was sent to the parents. As I have said, I hesitate a good deal to mention these circumstances to-day, largely on account of the fact that the 68th battalion, of which this boy was a member, very recently went to the front, and any person who might be able to make a defence of this case is not here to do so.
I wish to emphasize the point brought up by the junior member for Halifax with regard to the question of patronage. I have heard it stated in the House by the Minister of Militia that there was no. patronage list in the Department of Militia. Well,
I can only say this: The Militia Department and the Government have allowed the matter of patronage in connection with militia supplies to drift into the hands of local patronage committees. Although all persons, Liberals and Conservatives alike, are doing their share in the matter of enlisting and recruiting, sending their sons to the front-both parties in equal degree,
I -think-and contributing to patriotic and Red Cross funds, no person tout one who is on a certain side of politics in parts of

the country with which I am familiar can get anything to do at all. Surely, when all the people of the country -are spending all the money they can -afford and doing all they can in the interests of Canada's part in this war, it is time to- instruct these local patronage committees to leave party patronage alone and deal with matters on a business basis.

With regard to one
observation that the hon. gentleman made, I am quite convinced that he is entirely wrong. When men enlist they must be taken out in green squads and handled by non-commissioned officers. They cannot be taken out in large numbers; they are taken out in green squads whether at headquarters or in the outlying villages, and they have to spend a certain time there until they are licked into shape before they can be taken to Barriefield or some other place and put into a large body such as a battalion or brigade for the purposes of manoeuvres. The reason this plan was adopted, I am quite sure, is that squad drill is the beginning; it is the only possible way that a green man can learn anything. Non-commissioned officers, such as sergeants and corporals, are scattered throughout the country for that purpose. You could not take a great mob of green men and put them together at some large centre and go through large manoeuvres right off-it would be ridiculous; it could not be done. With regard to patronage, I was somewhat interested in that question, because Canadians-I do not know whether they db so more than any other people- have to fight against a tendency in the country to look to the loaves and fishes. Some people are inordinately green; we all know that.
Hear, hear.

They have to be fought against by both parties. They are without shame and entirely shameless. We have seen lots of them. They are only too eager to cut your throat if they can possibly do it. They do not make their objections in connection with those things that could be freely and openly and effectively answered; they always take up something by which they can stab you in the back. Our only answer to these people is to give them a good kicking. They are not worthy of being fought in the good old British way, with the fists; they should be simply spanked. Intellectually, and especially

morally, they are children. As a matter of fact, some people-I am not speaking of my own locality, you may rest assured- have more or less criminal instincts.

Where did you get
your experience?
I was out West two or three years ago.
You have some political friends out there.

However, it is not
necessary to enlarge upon the point; we know that it is a fact. Out of curiosity, I endeavoured to find out if there was any patronage in the war purchasing and other departments, and I found out that there was not.

Oh, oh.
Mr. KY'TE: Where did you look?

There is no question, Mr. Chairman, that there is only one way of doing business, and that is the business way. Tenders should be called for, and the public should be notified; then every thing is above board. If that has not been done, I have been unable to find out the contrary. I quite agree that if it has not been done, most certainly it ought to have been done.

I wish to refer to the matter brought up by the member for Regina with regard to the men being taken into the different battalions who are absolutely unfit. Men are taken in for some reason or other, in many cases because certain officers are anxious to get their company or battalion recruited to full strength in order that this may be to their credit and that they may secure permanent appointments. There are many cases where men are recruited and given uniforms, although they could not possibly pass the usual rigid examination that a man is called upon to undergo before he goes to the firing line. The result has been that in many cases men have been enlisted and trained for six months or a year, and then, on a more rigid examination before being sent to the front, have been rejected. This involves a tremendous and useless expense to the country. I knew that this was taking place, and my own knowledge was confirmed by the statement of a gentleman who went over with the first contingent as a junior officer and returned as a lieutenant colonel a year ago. He said that in some cases men who were suffering from some physical disabilities concealed those disabilities when enlisting, that they were not discovered by the medical examiners, and that, becoming tired of trench life after one or two months, these men made known their physical disabilities, and so were relieved of duty and sent home. In many cases these men had some injury, or had suffered from illness through their exposure in the trenches, and so they will become charges upon the people of Canada so long as they live. I would urge that the examination at enlistment be made much more rigid.
I think the hon. member will find that the present system is to examine the men viery closely on enlistment, and not to examine them again. I know that to be the. practice in my district.

I am aware that there has always been an examination of the men on enlistment, but in some cases where commanding officers are anxious to fill up their regiments men are accepted who are absolutely unfit physically, and who could not pass a rigid examination. While there has undoubtedly been some improvement, there is still room for further effort and further improvement along that line.
Is the hon. member aware that the regulations call for all of those things? The fault must lie with the examining officer.

That may be. I have no doubt that if all the regulations were lived up to things would be better. I am not bringing this matter up with any intention of complaining, but I am anxious to effect improvement and to save money. Could the Prime Minister, after eight o'clock, give us any idea oi the cost per man of the maintenance of our army in the field, including supplies, munitions and everything?
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

The terms of this resolution, as has already been stated by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, will be received without opposition; in fact, will be received with full accord in pursuance of the policy which has been adopted by men of all parties since the beginning of the war, of uniting, irrespective of political affiliations, to do all we can to help the Mother Country. In this connection, I would like to take
32&4

exception to a statement made by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister this afternoon as to there having been some wonderment, or doubt, before the war began as to whether Canada would be able to contribute as many men as she has contributed to the fighting forces. I do not pretend to be a prophet in any sense, but I always felt that there could never be any doubt whatever as to the attitude of the Canadian people when the interests of the Empire were at stake. Those of us who copse from people who have lived for two or three generations in Canada know that among the Canadian people there has always been the feeling that the little island which constitutes the seat of Empire was the home land, and although our patriotism may not have been very demonstrative, there was always the certainty that, under the conditions which prevail in Canada, under our democracy, and with the full realization of the issues of this war, there would be a response on the part of the people to whatever extent might be necessary to aid the Empire. I therefore assert that there need never have been any doubt whatever as to what Canada's response would be. There was certain to be a recognition of the conditions, and a gathering round the banner with that enthusiasm which we have seen manifested in all parts of this country. When it is said that it is a matter of particular wonderment that within three months of the outbreak of war, 30,000 men rushed to the colours, I would like to point out that no man and no party is entitled tc any particular credit, and that the wonderment has no justification whatever. The response simply proved the latent patriotism of the people of this land and was an expression of the realization of the tremendous issues at stake and of the people's attachment to our constitutional fabric. They rushed to the standard, just as their forefathers did in the days of yore, as a matter of course. They responded to the call of the Empire, and the proposition of sending them overseas was a mere matter of detail which could be worked out, as a matter of detail by any Administration or by any minister capaJble of attending to the business of the country.
I do not make that remark in any harsh or complaining spirit, but I think it is only right in the Parliament of this country we should have a full recognition of the fact that the Canadian people, with their aspirations and ambitions, were there, ready for the call; that they came of their own free will, that they went to the front, 
and are going and will go, to whatever extent the necessities of the situation demand. Recognizing these facts, realizing that the Government had to take the responsibility of administering the affairs of this country in war time, I say that the same spirit which actuated the men who volunteered, actuates hon. gentlemen in this House on both sides, without difference and without question. Hence it is that, with a free hand, we have given to the Government everything that they have asked for in the way of financial aid, and now this resolution comes to us and is received in the same spirit. While that is so, however, it is only right to say that the Canadian people expect from the 'Government a special regard for wise economy in the administration of affairs, and an honest administration in dealing with the expenditures which are committed to its care. Though a strict accounting is not looked for at this stage, the Government may rest assured that the time will come, and perhaps come speedily, when war's alarms are over, when a strict accounting will be demanded.
With regard to such questions as relate to the administration of affairs, and more particularly to the preparations for war, an idea was expressed to me recently with reference to the mobilization of troops, which, though it may be too late for the Government to seize, might, I think, have been recognized earlier. All through this country, from one end to the other, we had a militia organization built up. In some distracts there was a very strong interest and an intense local spirit manifested, and it seems to me that it is one of the unfortunate things connected with the mobilization of our troops that we have absolutely destroyed, so far as this war is concerned, if not forever, any spirit of enthusiasm in the Tanks of the militia corps in this country. The men who have gone to fight cannot come back and say that they went from the 28th, the 38th, or 78th Militia Corps, and when, in the days to come, we seek to perpetuate, as we must perpetuate in this country, a system of militia organization, there will be an entire lack of that enthusiasm for the old militia associations from which the men went to fight, because these militia corps have lost their identity altogether in the battalion_s that have been formed. We have heard references this afternoon to the number of officers who have qualified, and as to their selection for the particular corps in which they have served or are serving. The idea

ments were to go over as a Highland brigade, I say to the Prime Minister, now that he is Acting Minister mf Militia and Defence, that he should see that all obstacles to their going are removed and that a Highland brigade be formed, because, unless he does so, he will find that it will create a sense of disappointment throughout the province and a lack of enthusiasm when the call comes again, if it does come, for more recruits.
I do think that, there ought to be a more intimate connection, between the Militia Department and the people who are engaged in recruiting. In one of the recruiting efforts that took place in our province, we were told that although the band of a certain regiment, accompanied by its commanding officer, was going out to look after men, the few recruiting agents in that province would not undertake to pay the travelling expenses of that band. Local people were asked to contribute towards that purpose, even to feed them when they were on tour. That occurred to my knowledge in my own constituency. Of course, that is a matter of detail, but at the same time it means that somewhere in this marvellous organization, about which we have heard so much, and about which so much credit is claimed, not with any right, oh account of the reasons I gave at the beginning of my remarks, there ifc something -wrong. This sort of thing naturally chills the enthusiasm of our people. If we are going to have recruiting, let us have it looked after in a proper manner. Such absurd conditions as that ought not to be permitted. It may be, of course, that an incident of that kind arises from the action of some subordinate but more care should be exercised in the matter of recruiting. Everybody in this country who is interested in the war, and who is anxious to see its successful completion, and to see Canada playing her part, must realize that if you are going to interfere with the highest ideals of the men -who are going to this war as volunteers you are simply hampering the cause that you want to succeed. You can go into any part of the Dominion and tell men to forget the smaller issues of life and rise to an appreciation of their higher duty and the possibility of the greatest sacrifice, but if you are going to complicate that with conditions which absolutely explode any thought of idealism in regard to the matter the result will be unsatisfactory. That applies in regard to recruiting. It also applies

in regard to the question of patronage. ' My hon. friend told us to-night	that
there was no patronage in the	War
Purchasing Commission. I will tell him how it works out. You have a	proposition to recruit men and billet them in a certain locality. The quartermaster of the particular regiment is told in some mysterious way that when he goes into a particular section he must consult the man ,who has the patronage and therefore, when he goes to that district, he parcels out the supplies among men who are dictated by the man who has the patronage. This is not perhaps of great importance but it grates harshly on the sensibilities of the -man who is actuated by idealism. I have had it occur in my own constituency where no attempt whatever has been made to call for local tenders. What difference does it make after all who sells the sugar, or the meat, having regard to the higher conditions, but when you go into a small locality where people are making their living out of this business and where a man is made to realize that because he happens to be a Liberal he must be kept out of the opportunity of tendering for supplies, how much enthusiasm, how much idealism are you apt to get from -him? I will tell what occurred in my own constituency. A company was billeted in my own town. An officer of the 106th Regiment goes to the gentleman who has the patronage and proceeds to parcel out these things without asking anybody to submit tenders.. I called the attention of the Acting Minister of Militia to it, hot for any purpose of my own, but because' the matter was. remarked about among the people, and he promised to call for tenders. He. did 60 eventually. Why was it necessary for me to have done that? Why should not he, in the first instance, have issued instructions that it was. the duty of the officer, on going into any locality, to poet up notices inviting tenders? It seems to be a small matter and personally it does not make any difference to me, but my right hon. friend knows that when you are dealing in high ideals and you bring in small, tu'penny ha'penny politics, you cannot continue on the higher plane and that is where the shoe pinches. The same thing occurred in another constituency just as it has occurred all over Nova Scotia. The way in which patronage in regard to militia matters has been handled in the county of Cape Breton is a disgrace to the Administration and I ask my right hon. friend to 'look into it.

A matter was called to my attention within the last two days which I wish to bring to the 'attention of the right hon. gentleman. This is not a matter possibly that has to do with militia business but it is in reference to the question of hospitals. The gentleman who has the patronage there was going around to find out if this Government was going to take charge of the hospitals so that he would be able to dictate the men who should be employed iin these institutions. I would ask my right hon. friend, for the credit of our province, to make some inquiries in regard to the gentleman who has the patronage in the county of Cape Breton and 6ee whether or not this is the kind of idealism to hold out before the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What kind of
hospital was it?

It was under the
Hospital Commission, and this gentleman was inquiring whether or not this hospital was going to be taken over by the Government, with a view to making recommendations as to the people to look after it. The conduct of the gentleman who has the patronage in Cape Breton county is known all over the province of Nova Scotia, and my right hon. friend had better inquire into it.
There have also been cases of ill treatment of soldiers, and I wish to call my right hon. friend's attention to the case of Pte. Chapman in my own constituency. He was one of a company of the 106th Regiment in charge,of the Nova Scotia Steel Works, and on account of being absent without leave, was strung up by the hands under the direction of the commanding officer of the company. This fact became known to the men in the works, which are in close proximity, and they went in a body and demanded that the man be taken down. He was taken down; otherwise there would have been a very unpleasant time. An investigation has been held locally hy the people interested. I can see no reason why any Canadian should be treated in that way when he is under military discipline in any of our towns. I know that in the face of the enemy drastic measures can be taken to punish a man, but when the men are in our cities in Canada the most refractory case can always be given in charge; there is always recourse to imprisonment. But to string a man up by his hands for such an offence as being absent without leave, is something the people of this country will
not stand for, and one very unfortunate thing abput it is that it has a most injurious effect upon recruiting.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Is that the same case mentioned by the hon. member for Guysborough?

Yes, Pte. Chapman, of a company of the 106th Regiment in charge of the Nova Scotia Steel Works. I happened to be in my county the other day and heard of the case, and I am calling these matters to the attention of my right hon. friend because this affords an opportunity we have not had hitherto.
My right hon. friend has referred to the givirig of commissions, which was brought up by the hon. member for Halifax. Of course, I know it is difficult to deal with these commissions altogether apart from favoritism. The party in power will, of course, listen to the requests made by its political friends; I can see that it is difficult to evade that. But in some constituencies the process of log Tolling to get commissions is going on continually. I do not suppose my right hon. friend, with his burdens of office, has any occasion to deal with these matters at first hand, but I can give him instances of this sort of thing. I should prefer to do it privately, however, as there is no necessity for doing it in open Parliament. But my right hon. friend must realize that there have been abuses of that kindj and the hon. member for Halifax was perfectly justified in mentioning the matter. There is no question about it. Men suddenly become patriotic Canadians, and develop into paymasters, quartermasters, and holders of other non-oombatant positions Of every other kind, and the only evidence that you can possibly find why they should have been appointed is that ^omebody had pull and got them there. Nobody ever charged these men with exhibiting any great enthusiasm in the past for the body politic or for the preservation of the rights and liberties of the people. Their sudden appearance in positions of this kind, which do not call for personal exposure on the battlefield in the face of the enemy, indicates a public spirit that has developed a little too rapidly to be considered entirely honest. A certain amount of that kind of thing, I suppose, cannot be helped, but if it can be helped, it ought to be. I am speaking from the highest possible motives, and not with a desire to be partisan in my criticism. I know the gentleman who

has the patronage in my county has gone to certain gentlemen and said: I can get you made a major, or colonel, or something else. I have known, men, particularly this gentleman from Cape Breton that I have referred to, trying to remove men who were politically dangerous to him, by offering them commissions of one rank or another. So long as it is possible for that kind of thing to be done, what is the use of talking idealism to our people, or asking a man to come out and fight for liberty! Men are being granted commissions in exactly the same way as postmasters, or mail-carriers are being appointed- bringing the thing down to absolutely common clay. Surely this matter is deserving of some attention, and should be looked into.
The weakness of the medical officers is a thing I have had occasion to call attention to before. This, in our province, is largely a matter of political patronage pure and simple. I know an order was issued by the Militia Department not long ago changing the system, but it all rests with the colonel of the regiment as to who shall examine the men. A young man in Nova Scotia with a good old Scotch name, Findlay MacMillan-
Have you any Canadians down there, or do the people down there all come from other countries?
They are a good deal better than, my hon. friend from Peterborough.
He has enlisted.

My hon. friend from Peterborough belongs to the Paymaster Brigade, sitting down here in uniform and not doing a bit of work. I like to see men in uniform go out with their corps. We are all getting tired of my hon. friend's diatribes. This young man Findlay MacMillan was very anxious to serve his country. After being examined by the local doctor in New Glasgow, who passed him and told him he would have no difficulty in getting to the front, this young man sold his farm and everything belonging to him, and was sent down to Halifax to join the regiment. The doctor at Halifax discovered that his was a case of what is known as flat feet; that is, his instep had fallen. The doctor said he could not be taken, and the young man was ordered to return home. But he had sold his farm and everything he had, and had no place to go to. My at-

tention was called to the matter to-day in a letter from a friend of his, who described the situation as most unfortunate. There is evidence of incomplete medical inspection. Then there are oases' of men who have been sent overseas and have had to be sent back from England. This young man, Findlay MacMillan, was told by the doctor that he was all right, and he joined the army at considerable material loss to himself. He has now lost his ambition to go to the war, because he would not be allowed to go, and he is compelled to stay at home, with his occupation gone and with no home life. I do not know what remedy to suggest in this particular case, but I can give my right hon. friend all the facts, and I think they are worth inquiring into. I do not mean to say that the medical officer deliberately passed him in the first place, knowing he had flat feet, but that is just one example of improper medical inspection in the first . instance.
Another thing I would take the liberty of asking my right hon. friend is that he should tell the House frankly what the attitude of the Government is in regard *to returning money subscribed for machine guns. I think the House and the country are entitled to a full explanation of how that matter came before the people. Every one was startled at the announcement made by Senator Lougheed, then in charge of the Department of Militia and Defence, calling upon the people to contribute money to provide machine guns. Parliament had voted $150,000,000 for the very purpose of providing equipment, clothing, and other things including machine guns. For the moment I was at a loss, so far as my own constituency is concerned, to understand why the Government was asking the people to come to their relief in this matter. The newspapers, in the enthusiasm of the moment, called upon every one who was a patriot to subscribe to this fund. But what did Parliament vote $150,000,000 for if the people were to be appealed to to put their hands in their pockets for the purpose of providing machine guns?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To what appeal does the hon. gentleman allude?

To the appeal made in the Halifax Herald, for instance, my right hon. friend's own paper, asking all the people to contribute to this fund, and indicating those who did not .contribute were unpatriotic and disloyal.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: An appeal made by the Government?

Senator Lougheed
who was then, I think, acting Minister of Militia, had written a letter, which was published in that paper, calling upon the people to respond to this appeal. That appeal was made throughout our province, and certain municipalities passed resolutions in view of the demands made, appropriating money for this purpose. Patriotic organizations and individuals also contributed. I think we are entitled to know whether the Government intends to return the money thus obtained-. I put a question on the Order Paper asking a statement of the Government policy in regard to this matter. The Prime Minister answered me that he had given an answer to the question. I looked up Hansard, to which he referred me, and got very little satisfaction. What we want to know is whether the Government will return to the municipalities and individuals this money which should never h^ve been taken from them. And right here let me say a word in regard to this matter of people going up and down the country getting up subscriptions for this, that, and the other thing. The Government, through the Department of Militia, or some other department, should exercise supervision with regard to this. I was asked by some very estimable gentleman to join a delegation to wait upon the Minister of the Naval Service to ask the Government to give a subscription to the Seamen's Fund of Great Britain. I said at once that I would do nothing of the kind, for coming from one of the provinces by the sea I knew something of the conditions, and I knew that this was not a war fund at all. There does not exist in Great Britain such machinery as we have, to provide marine hospitals and to care for sailors. Some well-intentioned person had started this propaganda by which everybody in Canada was to be asked to contribute to this fund and the Government was to be asked to make a special contribution; but the fund is purely local in its character and is dealt with entirely by people on the other side of the water. I was glad to find that my hon. friend the Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Hazen), in discussing this matter before the Pension Committee, agreed absolutely with the position I had taken. This is an illustration of the kind of appeals that are being made all over Canada today. I feel that it is the duty of the Government to have some supervision over these appeals, which, no doubt, are made by well-intentioned people, to the generosity of our
folks who, thinking they are contributing to some good cause, give a lot of money to objects some of which ultimately turn out to be of no value. Take, for instance, the appeal made at the beginning of the war for a hospital ship, which movement was started in Toronto. Those who understood these matters knew there was no real advantage in that movement, and yet over $100,000 was raised. And so it goes on. I ask that those municipalities and individuals who so wish should be refunded the money they contributed toward the purchase of machine guns. It would be just as reasonable to start a public subscription to buy rifles, or clothing, for the troops. It is a regrettable thing that these subscriptions should have been asked for apparently under official sanction.
In connection with thi6 war vote, I wish to call the Prime Minister's attention to a situation which exists in our province with reference to what might properly be called a naval matter, the commandeering of ships. Newfoundland has made the very strongest representations to the Mother Country with regard to what they allege to have been discrimination in the commandeering of ships, and these representations, I understand', have had some effect. Here in Canada what is the result of this commandeering? In regard to our coal, companies, the total number of ships engaged in the coal trade between Nova Scotia and Montreal have been Commandeered, and ^et, you can go out and charter vessels at enormous rates which sail under the British flag. Why should that be? Why. should this coal industry in our province be seriously interfered with; why should the city of Montreal be put to a disadvantage through not being -able to get coal from Nova Scotia, and why should the American coal people be given a chance tp get a foothold in the Montreal market, by the removal of the ships engaged in the coal trade while there -are ships flying the British flag which can be chartered at very high rates?
Canada is doing her level best in this war. The very be^t of our men have gone to the front. And in discussing this matter, we .should never forget the splendid enthusiasm exhibited by the women of Canada, which is even greater than that of the men. The women have been called upon to make great sacrifices in giving up sons and husbands and dear ones-and the son is generally dearer to the mother than to the father. The devotion ot our women

will never be forgotten. The people of Canada have made marvellous sacrifices, and are prepared to make more. But we must realize that, as far as possible, we should keep our house in order, we should keep an eye to the future. If there is, as I say there is, a condition under which one of our greatest industries is being paralyzed for want of ships, if there are other vessels available which could be commandeered, those other vessels ought to be taken first.
This resolution provides for expenditures in the Naval Department. I am sorry to see that the hon. Minister of the Naval Service (Mr. Hazen) is not here. I am sure that I voice the sentiment of every hon. gentleman on this eide of the House when I say that our hearts go out to him in sympathy on account of the death of his boy. Such an event as thiat saddens every one and stills the voice of faction. I .am sure that every hon. member in the House extends to my hon. friend the deepest sympathy in the great loss he has sustained. '
I was proceeding to refer to the Naval Service. I am glad to see that within the last week or two we have been getting evidence of the truth of the statement which I made earlier in the session; that Great Britain needed men upon the sea. I was told in this Parliament since the House opened this session that Great Britain did not need men upon the sea. I know the facts, and I knew that I was correct. We have been glad to see men wearing the blue uniform of the navy amongst us; it is evidence that Great Britain does desire men on the sea, and these naval men are recruiting for that purpose. If the Minister of Naval Service were here I would ask him at the earliest possible date to. make a statement, as to the kind and number of men that Great Britain wants from us, so that the facts may be placed properly before those who are in a position to respond to the call. I am quite sure that that call for men for the navy will be responded to by our hardy and brave sea-faring Canadians in as great degree as the call for men to serve the Empire on land.
I noticed the other day an advertisement in some of the local papers which purported to come from my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, encouraging the people to patriotism and production and embodying some other propaganda. It is a desirable thing, of course, to patronize the press of the country, but I would like to know from my right hon. friend whether or not expenditures in that line and in connection with

the pamphlets we have seen in regard to the subject come out of this vote? I am quite sure that the people who live on the farms need no incentive to produce all they can, and that there will be no lack of response from all classes of our people in regard to this question of production. One, of the strange features of the war is that the agriculturists of Canada are able to get higher prices than they ever got /before for .all staple lines of production. SO it is with most of the other things that enter into the necessaries of life, These things wil be produced, and I do not know that it is evidence of economy that there should be any special .publication of books to call forth the most ordinary business efforts from the agriculturists or from any other class of people in onr country. The idea that has been promulgated, that the people of Canada | were not ready to assist the Empire in this war in every possible way, is a delusion. While Canada was not playing a 'brass band at the front door before the war, shouting her patriotism as some other colonies or nations were, she was ready to assist the Old Land whenever necessity arose. No pumping up of enthusiasm was necessary; no political efforts were required in order to get a response. Freely and generously from every province of this great Dominion the boys came forth and have gone to fight. The same feeling of devotion exists in connection with our industrial and agricultural life, and I am quite sure that everything that is necessary will be forthcoming, to the extent of our resources, and that it will come without any particular pumping or fostering or unnecessary expenditure.
I have endeavoured to bring to. the attention of my .right hon. friend some matters that seem to he of importance in connection with this resolution, and I submit them with the hope that they will receive his fullest consideration.

The hon. member for Pictou has just mentioned the fact that officers of the British Navy are here recruiting for the British Admiralty. I am very pleased to hear that. In connection with the Navy, I wish to inform my right hon. friend that I clipped from one of the New York papers a few days ago the following :
San Francisco, April, 27.-According to unconfirmed advices received at the Mare Island Navy Yard today, the American power schooner Oregon, owned by the Crowley Launch and. Tugboat Company of San Francisco, has been

seized by the British cruiser Rainbow in the Gulf of California.
The Oregon sailed from San Francisco last June, under charter to the German firm of Linga and Company of Mazatlan. At that time she carried a cargo of lumber. It was understood the vessel was to be used in the west coast trade. Nothing is known here of her recent movements.
I would like to ask my right hon. friend if that report is confirmed? If it is, it is one other exploit on the part of the much despised Canadian navy. As one of the fathers of that navy, I rejoice greatly that the Rainbow and the Niobe are proving true to their fathers.

I
wish to say a few words upon the resolution now before the committee, and particularly with regard to my own province. I am under the impression that the percentage of recruiting in the province of Prince Edward is not as large as in some of the western provinces of Canada, but the reason is very easily understood. The province being purely agricultural, the young men, as soon as they come to manhood, go either to the United States or to western Canada in large numbers, leaving just enough men at home to work the farms. Consequently, those of military age and ability are not as numerous there as they are in some of the other provinces, particularly in the West, where they get the young and the healthy, the strong and the energetic from the other provinces and from the Old Country as well. Notwithstanding that fact, however, I believe that the percentage of recruiting in the province of Prince Edward Island is very good. Moreover, the people subscribed liberally to every appeal that was made to them. In that connection I wish to refer to the appeal that was made on behalf of the fund that was needed to buy machine guns. When it was stated that the troops at the front were handicapped to a very great extent by not having a sufficient number of machine guns, the people thought that if they would subscribe money to that fund the defect could be remedied. An appeal went out at that time, from the Acting Minister of Militia, Senator Lougheed, that it would be very acceptable to the Government and the Militia Department if money should be obtained for that purpose. To show how that appeal was received in the province and even in the town from which I come, the people of the town provided money to purchase three guns. One man subscribed enough to purchase a machine gun; he happened to be in a position
to do so easily. Another citizen in very moderate .circumstances, feeling the necessity of doing everything he could, subscribed for another gun. Then the town provided another, and this citizen who, as I say, is in very moderate circumstances, gave $300 more for the second gun. Everybody subscribed, even the school children, who offered their small savings of fifty, sixty, or seventy cents, or a dollar. In a very short time sufficient money was subscribed for three machine guns. It has been the same with every other fund, the Belgian relief, the Red Gross, the Patriotic fund, the Field Army Service fund, every fund was subscribed to generously. I think that, instead of showing organization in the Militia Department, the appeal for funds to purchase machine guns shows a lack of organization. It should not have been necessary for the department to appeal to the patriotic impulses of the people in order to provide money to purchase one of the most necessary articles for troops at the front.
With regard to the patronage list, to which the Prime Minister referred this afternoon, the right hon. gentleman no doubt thinks he is stating the facts. But, as a matter of fact, he is far astray; he is misinformed, because so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, and I presume conditions are very similar in other provinces, there is nothing but a patronage list. A Liberal has no more chance of providing any supplies for the troops stationed at local headquarters than if he were a man belonging to a foreign country. I have now a question on the Order Paper, and if it is answered satisfactorily and truthfully I shall be able to give names that I am sure will satisfy the Prime Minister of the accuracy of my statements. I say truthfully, because I find that questions which I put on the Order Paper and which were answered earlier in the season were not answered correctly, and I have the proof under my hand. On February 3, this question was answered by the Minister of Militia and Defence:
Mr. J. J. Hughes:
1.	What procedure is followed to obtain supplies for the troops at local headquarters?
2.	Are tenders asked for by public advertisement, or is there a patronage list, and are the parties whose names are on the patronage list asked to submit offers?
3.	Is there a patronage list for Prince Edward Island?
4.	If so, who prepared the list for the Government, what are the names and addresses of the parties on the list, and who recommended these names to the Government or the purchasing committee?



Sir Sam Hughes:
1.	The practice followed in making contracts for supplies to the troops at the various mobilization centres throughout Canada varies according to circumstances. If there is time enough before the supplies are required, tenders are called for by public advertisement, usually by posters put up in and about the town where the troops are to be stationed. When the time is too short to allow this to be done, tenders are obtained by circular letter or telegram from Ottawa, addressed to dealers of the locality concerned. Names of dealers are supplied by War Purchasing Committee. In some cases where the time is very short, the officer commanding the district is authorized to procure tenders from local concerns and transmit them, by mail or telegraph, to Ottawa for approval. No application from responsible parties for permission to tender is refused; and tender forms and necessary information are supplied to all such applicants. In all cases, the lowest tenders received are accepted.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	No.
4.	Answered by No. 3.
That is a very satisfactory explanation; but, strange to say, according to letters I have received from reputable people, not a Liberal has been found to provide any supplies in the carrying out of this arrangement. Let me come down to a concrete case. I shall take the article of milk. On the 16th of February this question was answered:
Mr. Hughes:
1.	Where is the milk obtained that is supplied to the troops at Charlottetown, P.E.I. ?
2.	Is it fluid or powder milk, and what price is paid for it?
3.	How is powder milk made, and is there any cream in it?
Sir Sam Hughes:
1.	From J. Tobin & Co., Halifax, N.S.
2.	(a) Powder milk. (b) 14i cents per pound.
3.	(a) By a superheated process .	(b)
Powder milk which is the solids of milk with the water evaporated containing 23.8 per cent of fat which returns to its original element by the addition of water.
Parties who obtained some of that powdered milk 'had it analysed
9 p.m. in Charlottetown and found that it contained no fat at all, although this answer says it contained 23 per cent. I had a sample of it analysed here at Ottawa by Mr. C. H. Robinson. Hie report was as follows:
Central Experimental Farm,
Ottawa, March 16, 1916.
J. J. Hughes, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir,-In the absence of Dr. Shutt I beg to hand you my report on the sample of milk powder forwarded by you on the 6th Instant.

Analysis.
Moisture		2.86

The undertermined consists almost entirely of milk sugar.
The analysis corresponds to that of powder made from skim or separated milk. One pound of this milk powder added to nine pounds of water would give a milk closely approximating in composition to that of skim or separated milk obtained from dairymen.
