Assistant Chemist.
There is a factory in Charlottetown that manufactures condensed milk.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Where did the hon. member get that report?
From Mr. C. H. Robinson, assistant chemist at the experimental farm.
You should have got Borden's condensed milk.

This factory at Charlottetown makes condensed mi'lk which is sold all over Canadd, and is used in construction, mining and lumber camps. It is whole milk and is sold at from 10 to 11 cents a pound, yet that factory could not supply -a pound of milk to the troops at Charlottetown, while the department were buying skimmed milk in Halifax at 14^ cents a pound. They were not personae gratae to the [Patronage Committee. I am informed by reputable people that hardly a Liberal in Charlottetown is supplying anything to the troops, and I understand That the same condition prevails at Summerside.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was there not a public call for tenders?
I do not know about that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am informed by the Deputy Minister of Militia that there *was a public call for tenders,

I do not know what the tenders call for. I saw one of the forms of tender, and it called for powdered -milk. I do net know whether that was the form used in this ease or not; if it was, of course, that factory could not supply it, because it does not deal in, that class of article. It deals in a much better article, and _could supply it at a lower price, at, as I have said, from 10 to 11 cents per pound. At the town of Souris, where 150 soldiers are located, I understand that the officers in charge made some inquiries of different

people with regard to supplies, and, as a matter of fact, Conservatives are supplying the articles. I am told-I cannot state positively whether this is correct or not, although I have the information from a reputable source-that it has been found -that the supplies are about 20- per cent short of weight, and if that can be done- and I am given to understand that a somewhat similar condition exists in other parts of the province-and favoured parties can supply short weights of course they can put in low tenders.
Can you give us the names of any parties who supplied short weights?
They must have been among the men supplying the goods.
I wish to draw the attention of the Prime Minister-
I have asked the hon. gentleman a question; I have asked whether he can give us the names of any of those farmers who are supplying short weights.
I have a question on the Order Paper asking for that information, and as soon as I get it I will give it to my hon. friend.
Appoint a commission.

In connection with the
Militia Department, advertisements have been published asking for students for the Militia College at Kingston. This is in connection with the war and I have here a particular instance of a' Liberal newspaper published in Charlottetown which was not allowed to publish that advertisement. That paper, I know, took an active part in promoting everything connected with the war, publishing freely notices calling meetings for recruiting purposes, and notices in connection with subscription funds, and doing everything that every other newspaper in the province did. In fact, there were no party lines drawn, so far as the people were concerned. Liberals and Conservatives alike have been eager and anxious to do their bit all over the Dominion, and it is the same in the province of Prince Edward Island as in other provinces. And yet this advertisement, calling for young men to attend the Military College, which is supported by the people, for the purpose of qualifying themselves to defend their country in case of need, was withheld from this newspaper. I can give the names
in this instance, but I presume the officers of the Milita Department are well aware that I am stating a fact.
In regard to the medical officers employed in connection with the Army Service, I have this to say: A medical man in Charlottetown, who held a position in the active militia, and whose son or nephew has already given up his life in defence of his country, has not been allowed to examine a single recruit for active service. He has been turned down, although he was an officer in the active militia before the war broke out. These are some of the things that are being done all over the country.
Something has been said here to-day with regard to the surplus of officers in the Old Country, and in Canada. I have information to the effect that there are about 600 officers now in Great Britain who are not employed. I might as well state how I came by that information. Just a few days ago, in the Queen Hotel in Halifax, I happened to be sitting at a table when two officers were discussing the matter. They put it in this way:	They said that there
were 600 Canadian officers " canned " in Great Britain, 600 officers who had nothing to do. They 'appeared to know what they were talking albout. They also said that there were enough officers in the Dominion of Canada to supply an army of one million men, many of them striplings, some of them boys of from 18 to 20 years of age, who would have nothing to do, and for whom there was no possibility of employment; mere boys who could not be placed in charge of troops. A peculiar condition of things, in this connection exists even in this Parliament where we see men in khaki who evidently are not going to the front. Early in this session I myself had an invitation to become an officer. Now, there would be no more chance of my going to the front, or of being of any use as an officer, than of taking a trip to the moon.
Hear, hear.

I would be just as qualified as some men who sit in this House in khaki, and who are in receipt of pay as officers as well as of their indemnity as members. According to a return brought down, their wives are also in receipt of a separation allowance. That is a matter which should receive some consideration. Is there any limit to the demands that are to be made upon the war appropriation fund? If there are 500 or 600 officers in Great Britain who are on the pay roll and

who are doing nothing there; if there are enough officers in Canada to supply an army of a million men, all of whom are on the pay roll, and if there are men sitting in this Parliament who will never by any possibility go to the front, who know they will not go, who never expected to go, and who are in receipt of pay while their wives receive a separation allowance, is it reasonable to suppose that when the people know these things they will be as generous with their subscriptions to the war funds ,as they would be if these matters were conducted properly and honestly and economically as they ought to be. Taken individually, these things are perhaps small, but in the aggregate they amount to a good deal.
There are things that ought to be looked into. I am going to give you concrete cases. The- Prime Minister is not well in-. formed when he states there is no patronage list in this country. He stated this afternoon that as far as he knew there was no patronage list, and in that he may be correct, but I say again that he is not well informed, because every man who- reads that statement will know that it is not correct. The patronage list, in so far as the war is concerned, is just as active as it is in regard to any civil matter in the Government service. It is so in the province from which I come, and I presume it is so in other provinces.
No.

Perhaps not. Well, so much the better. The patronage system should not prevail in any province. The whole of the people of Canada are doing all in their power to win this great war. Liberals just as well as Conservatives, are volunteering, going to the front, they are willing to shed their blood, willing to sacrifice their lives, willing to do everything in their power, and patronage should have no place in a matter of this kind. Now that the Prime Minister is taking a more active part in the expenditure of the money appropriated for war purposes than he has done heretofore, we will probably have a better condition of affairs. I heard that a paymaster at one of the headquarters in Ontario, whose accounts were examined and found not to be correct, was sent to Great Britain as a paymaster at a greatly increased salary.

It is time for a change, it is time that an improvement should be made, because every person in my province knows that I am stating facts. I regret to have to state them. We will look for better things if the Prime Minister pays more attention to these matters than he has been able to pay in the past.

I
do not intend to take up very much time of the committee, but I would like to say a few words in regard to the resolution that is now before the House to provide for the war appropriation for the coming year. In doing so I do not desire to assume the role of a critic or to say anything that would seem harsh or unnecessary in regard to the carrying on of our part of the war. But I do want to draw the attention of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), who is now looking after the Department of Militia and Defence, to some matters that I think are of interest to the people as a whole, and which are of interest to the Government of which he has the honour to be the head. Much has been said this afternoon, while this resolution has been under discussion, in regard to matters that have Come to the attention of hon. members in different parts of the Dominion concerning the carrying on of the war insofar as Canada is concerned. One particular criticism was brought to the attention of the committee to-night of which I heartily approve, and that was in regard to the officers that are being appointed to carry on recruiting and to train and control the men in the regiments -I will not say throughout Canada, because I do not know if this criticism will apply to all parts of the country-but I will say down near my own home in the Maritime Provinces. We all know that a very large number of men have been appointed to responsible positions in connection with the training of recruits and the raising of battalions, without due regard to their military qualifications. These men are selected-I do not want to say without any regard to their fitness for the position-but I do know of many instances where men have been selected and placed in charge of battalions who have not had the slightest military experience before they

put on the King's uniform, and have been made captains and quartermasters in different battalions in the Maritime Provinces. I do not say this because I have any personal feeling against these men. They may be imbued with the most patriotic sentiments, but while that may be true it does not impress the country; it does not impress the young men; it does not impress the men whom we are seeking to enlist in the Canadian army that officers should be selected from people of this class. They are selected from three standpoints, and three standpoints alone-social influence, financial influence and political influence. That is the way selections are made of officers in the Maritime Provinces very largely.

I am not here to say that there have been no Liberals appointed but I am here to complain that there have been a large number of officers appointed in the Maritime Provinces who have not had the slightest experience and who are	no
more fitted to be majors, captains or quarter-masters than I am, and I have
not had the slightest experience in the world. .My hon. friends have mentioned a number of things in regard to the treatment of soldiers who have been punished for lapses in conduct. As far as I am personally concerned I admire the man who takes upon himself the duties of citizenship and enlists as one of our soldiers to go forth and do his part in this war. I admire and respect that man. I believe, however, that you cannot carry on a war, or properly train soldiers without a certain amount of discipline. It is absolutely necessary that there should be proper discipline, but while I admife discipline I detest military snobbishness, and there is a great deal of that in this country at the present time. Just because a man happens to be an officer and holds a little higher rank than somebody else has, he has no right to abuse his authority in the way a number of military officers are doing in this country. The punishments that have been meted out to soldiers in the ranks have been reported in the newspapers, and are absolutely true.

gentleman any other instances of that kind?

I have no instances of that
kind to,give. I am not speaking from my own knowledge of the harsh treatment some of the privates receive from their officers. The point I am making is that, the privates are very often treated as if they were far below the officers. We are all Canadians, and the private may come from just as good a family and have just as good blood in his veins as the officer who happens to have been chosen through influence; and simply because an officer has that influence is no reason why the private should be abused and trampled upon, as they are in many training camps throughout the country.
With regard to this vote, I am sure there is not a member of tills House but who intends to vote it cheerfully. At the same time I think it devolves upon us, as representing the people of this country, to demand that the money shall be honestly and reasonably expended for the purpose for which it is intended. No one, I am sure, could have occupied a seat in this House for even so short a time as I have, and heard the evidence given at meet-
32G6

ings of the Public Accounts Committee, without coming to the conclusion that the money that has been voted for war purposes during the last two years .has not all been expended with that degree of care that should have been exercised. A number of instances have been given, and tonight I wish to draw .the attention of my right hon. friend to an expenditure which has been much talked about in the province of New Brunswick, near my home town. I know the location very well; it is in the constituency of my hon. friend the member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes), and I may say that we live very happily together in adjoining towns. If the statements that have been made by a large number of people in that constituency, and that have appeared in the press, in regard to the expenditure of a sum of money last year in the preparation of a building for the billetting of the soldiers in that particular town are true an investigation should certainly be held, to ascertain whether or not this large amount of money was, not to use a harsher term, absolutely wasted. If the reports in regard to the expenditure of that sum of money in the constituency of my hon. friend are true, and if his attitude on patronage is what he publicly stated it to be at the Forum the other night, then I must congratulate him for having had a very sudden change of heart in regard to the -patronage system. I hold in my hand a reputable paper published in the province of New Brunswick, which makes very serious charges with regard to the expenditure of public money in the county of Cumberland, for the purpose of fitting up a building to accommodate the soldiers who were in training there in the year 1915. The editor of this paper is a responsible gentleman, both financially and otherwise, and claims to have made a careful personal examination into the matter. Several times .he has demanded an investigation, and is prepared to prove his statements. I shall read a few of the charges he makes, but I might first of all say that although we have plenty of lumber close to Cumberland county, while the lumber that was used in this building was purchased some distance away, in the county of Hants, and brought over two railway lines to Amherst. We must not forget that there were already two public buildings in Amherst which could have [DOT] been used-the armoury and the winter fair building. However, they fitted up these barracks for the soldiers at the extraordin-
ary cost of between $25,000 and $30,000. The soldiers remained in the building only a few months, and last winter it was dismantled, .and the soldiers quartered in another place. If this is true it was certainly an extravagant expenditure, to use no harsher term. After the building had been fitted up, then arose the question as to provisions, groceries, meats, and hay and oats, because horses were to be billeted there as well as soldiers. The Prime Minister said this afternoon that he had not 'heard there were any patronage lists. He did not say there were none; I am sorry he was not able to say that. If he had attended the meetings of the Public Accounts Committee this session he would have heard the Director of Contracts state under oath that there was a patronage list in the Militia Department, and that it had been prepared shortly after the election of 1911, and that the material required by the department was purchased from persons whose names appeared on that list. Whether he was mistaken or not, I cannot say; I do not know anything to the contrary; but I can tell the Prime Minister that if he does not know that there are patronage lists, he is not aware of what takes place in different constituencies throughout the country when supplies and provisions are purchased for the maintenance of the troops. I know what takes place in my portion of the country.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that these supplies are not ah purchase*! subject to public tender?

subject to public tender. Further, in certain localities the patronage is not merely confined to the Conservative party, but it is confined to an inner ring of that party, the ordinary Conservatives being excluded, and only a very select few allowed to tender for supplying the troops.
. Public tenders were never called by advertisement it is reported.
There was a farce of private tendering.
Even these forms of tender it is said, were only to be had at one office, and only by those not only of the right political stripe but within the ring.
For instance, a leading hay dealer of Amherst, who happened to be a Liberal, tried to get a chance to tender on the hay (to be" provided for the horses.) He was told
That $17 a ton would be highway robbery and anyway he could not get a chance to tender because he was of the wrong political stripe. Within a week the contract for hay was awarded to one of the ring at $21 per ton.
One of the leading meat supply firms of Amherst desired to tender for the beef required. One of the members of this firm was a strong supporter of Mr. Rhodes at the last election, but he was not in the ring and although he made repeated applications for a chance to tender on the beef he failed to get an opportunity of doing so. He was told by one of the ring that beef should be supplied for about eleven cents a pound, but within a few days the contract was awarded to the same man who got the hay contract at the price of fourteen cents per pound. This gentleman made a contract with the Harris Abbatoir Company of Hamilton, Ont., to supply him with beef required at ten and a half cents a pound delivered in Amherst. As there was used between 1,500 and 2,000 poqnds per day it can be seen that there was a profit of somewhere between $52,50 and $70 per day in beef alone.
There are several large bakeries in Amherst and although their proprietors had -worked hard for Mr. Rhodes at the last election and spent their time and money in his interests they were outside of the ring and were passed by. The contract was given to a wholesale grocer.
The contract for vegetables was given to this same wholesale grocer at an extravagant price (although he was not engaged in the vegetable business) and who sub-let it to a lesser member of the ring.
The contract for coal was given, without tender, to the proprietor of an ice-cream parlor and oyster saloon, who up to that time had
never been engaged in the coal business but the price he received was encouraging to say the least.
Now, even suppose that these statements are incorrect, some investigation should be held, for these allegations go forth to the country and if they are incorrect they do a great injustice to those in charge of these matters. But the people are very sensitive in regard to the expenditure of these war appropriations. They might not care for a few dollars in regard to ordinary expenditures; but when they realize that day after day and week after week they are called upon at every street corner to subscribe to good causes in connection with the war- and they are glad to give what they can afford to give-and when they are told that money is being squandered and wasted, not to use a harsher name, in patronage contracts given to friends of the Government, the contrast between the sacrifices they are making and the unjust advantage which others are gaining arouses the keenest dissatisfaction. The people expect a square, honest, careful expenditure of the money voted by this Parliament to the Govern- . ment for the carrying on of this war. The Prime Minister this afternoon said that he did not knoyv of any patronage list from which provisions were purchased for the Militia Department. Now, saying nothing of the past, however unfortunate it may be that we have been extravagant-for the. past is gone-I would ask the Prime Minister to go a step further and say that if there is a patronage list at the present time there should be no patronage list in the future, so far as concerns the expenditure of the money passed under this resolution. I have felt it my duty to call the attention of the committee to instances of what is believed to be extravagance in the expenditure of money voted for the war.
I hope that in the future greater care will be exercised and that we shall have a better report in regard to the expenditure of the money now to be voted than we have had in regard to the money voted in former years.

cumstance that being chairman of committees I am debarred from taking an active part in the debate. I certainly should not have spoken under ordinary conditions, but I could not sit quietly in the chair and listen to wild, outrageous, and absolutely unfounded assertions as I shall be able to show them to be. I cannot at the moment speak from the documents, for I have not them with me, but I might have had them here had I had notice that I should be called upon to deal with these charges. The hon. member has been entirely misinformed. When troops were first brought to Amherst, there was a certain urgency in the matter of securing tenders as it was supposed that the troops would be brought there at an earlier date than they were. At that time, a supply officer of the Department came and left with me certain tender forms, asking me to submit these to various contractors in my constituency. Now, I wish to state the case exactly as it happened. I made particular inquiry of him as to whether this was the method which had obtained in the department, and he told me it was the method that had obtained for many years. I wish to assume entire responsibility for the manner in which these contract forms were at that time distributed. I took care, having regard to the system which had obtained in this country, that these tenders were handed to my political friends and not to my political opponents. I am not here to defend that	system.
I deplore the patronage	system.
I believe that it is a canker which is eating into the body politic of this country and I am willing to assist in every possible way in an attempt to eradicate it. That was the system which obtained, however, and I took care that tender forms were at that time placed in the hands of those who had been my political supporters. That is what hon. gentlemen opposite would do; that is what hon. gentlemen apposite have done; that is what I did, having regard to the circumstances, and knowing that that was the system which had obtained up to that time. But I did not approve of the system-and I have discussed the matter since on various occasions with different responsible officers of the Militia Department. Excepting those contracts which were awarded in the first instance, every contract in the constituency which I have the honour to represent has been awarded on open contract and by competition. As an evidence of that let me 
say that the very man whom the hon. member for Westmorland referred to a short time ago as not receiving a contract in the first instance is to-day the meat contractor in the town of Amherst, and he was a violent opponent of mine in the last political contest, but I find no fault with that. I have had absolutely nothing whatever to do directly or indirectly, with the awarding of contracts in the constituency of Cumberland since that first and only case. Troops have been quartered in the town of Springhill for several months. I wish to tell the hon. member for Westmorland that I do not know the name of a single contractor in the town who is supplying foodstuffs to the troops. At the request of the War Purchasing Commission, which did not receive a sufficient number of tenders in response to advertisements which were posted in public places in Springhill, I gave the name of every merchant in that town, Liberal and Conservative. The statement that I make in respect of the town of Springhill is absolutely true in respect of the town of Amherst; I do not know who the contractors are in Amherst to-day. I happen to know something about the meat contract because of some peculiar conditions that arose, and in regard to which I made particular inquiries. I was not consulted in any shape or form with respect to the awarding of contracts, and I state my absolute belief that they were awarded aftei competition and to the lowest tenderer.
My hon. friend drew some evidences of mirth from some hon. gentlemen on his side of the House by stating that a certain coal contract had been awarded to an ice-cream vendor, a man, he said, who had never been in the coal business. This ice-cream vendor, to my certain knowledge, has been in the coal business for at least ten years. He sells coal to the public in the town of Amherst to-day and he has done so in the years gone by. I do not think because a man happens to sell a few quarts of ice-cream or any other commodity that he should be debarred from selling coal. It seems to me that the two important considerations are: Was the coal of good quality, and was it sold at a fair price?
I notice, too, that the hon. member for Westmorland skated on thin ice when he discussed the question of lumber supplies. .He did not tell the committee that the company which supplied lumber was one of which I am president and in the stock of which I hold a fifth interest. I do not think that this is a matter to be hidden. As a matter of fact, it is well known that

I am in the lumber business and have been for a great many years:	I was very glad
indeed to find out, for the first time after the contract had been awarded, that a contract had been given to the company of which I am president. I am in the lumber business and I do not see why, becauses I am a member of Parliament that the company with which I am connected should be debarred from doing a certain amount of legitimate business, provided the company has lumber to sell and sells it at a fair price.
I do not purpose going into that matter further than to say that the lumber was, I believe, of fair quality and that it was sold at a fair price. By reason of its being dried in the open air it really had to be purchased from that company at ' that time, having regard to the fact that a large quantity was required at a season of the year when that quality of lumber could not be purchased from mills which had sold and shipped their whole cut.
I want to make the assertion positively, so that there can be no misunderstanding in respect to it, that so far as the constituency of Cumberland is concerned-I can speak only of that constituency, because I have not been concerned with outside constituencies-every contract for supplies is awarded on open tender and absolutely without respect to a man's political qualifications. I do not think the hon. member for Westmorland would have made the rash statements that he did make if there did not happen to be within the precincts of the building to-night one of the most prominent Liberals in my constituency. The hon. member for Westmorland has probably had a prod from him; that gentleman wished to take home with him some statement that Rhodes wa? getting a little bit of criticism in the House of Commons. There is in the constituency which 1 represent a newspaper which was founded solely and entirely for partisan purposes;
I refer to the Amherst Guardian an out and out Liberal sheet. That paper, published in my constituency, has not published any such statements as are published in the paper which my hon. friend has read. He reads from a paper which is published in his constituency, some 50 miles from the town in which I live. That paper would not dare publish such statements in the constituency in which I live. The hon. member made an appeal here to-night, as if, perforce, he were being shut off in the matter of investigation. Does he not know that the Prime Minister did something that was never heretofore done
in the Dominion of Canada-never done, so far as I know, in any British country before? He established a Royal Commission, with a roving commission, travelling up and down the length and breadth of this country and inviting people to lay charges against the Administration. That commission was in the province of Nova Scotia, and I myself caused an editorial to be published in the Amherst Daily News, a paper which is friendly to myself, inviting any one who had a charge to make in that constituency to bring it before the commission. Did they do so? Not at all. Then, does my my hon. friend forget that there is a Public Accounts Committee in the House of Commons? It is the easiest thing in the world for him to have these various matters investigated, and I may say that I shall be only too happy to assist him. If there is anything wrong in the manner in which this Government business has been conducted in my constituency, I want to know it, not for partisan purposes, but in the public interest, and I am just as anxious to know it as my hon. friend is. I repeat that I shall assist him in full measure if he will cause these matters to be brought before the Public Accounts Committee; I welcome an opportunity of having them investigated.
Troops were brought to Amherst in the first instance, and they were quartered in the building of the Canada Car and Foundry Company. I have no interest in the Canada Car and Foundry Company; I do not own a dollar's worth of stock, nor does any member of my immediate family.
I have no interest directly or indirectly in it, except that I happen to be local solicitor for the company-I say that only in passing. I wanted to see troops brought to Amherst because of the peculiar conditions at that time. Following the industrial depression, large buildings suitable for the accommodation of troops were vacant, anu the quartering of a regiment in the town at that time would have been of great lofad benefit. Amherst is strategically located as the geographical centre of the Maritime Provinces; the military authorities at Halifax were only too happy to see the troops brought into Amherst, and I was only too happy to lend my assistance to their being brought there. They were given the use of the buildings of the Canada Oar and Foundry Company, without the cost of one dollar by way of charge. The company have asked to be reimbursed for certain expenditures to which they were put, but there has been no charge for rental of the

However, the answer is open to my hon. friend, because this matter has been the subject of various questions by him, and I think others during this and the previous session. But it must be borne in mind that while the winter fair building was available for the use of the troops at that time, the military authorities then decided not to use that building for this reason:	Quarters were
being fitted up at that time for the 22nd French-Canadian Battalion, which came from Quebec, and also for the 6th Mounted Rifles, and for the use of the 6th Mounted Rifles it was necessary to have a building where 750 horse stalls could be built for the accommodation of their horses. There was no building within a mile of the winter fair building which could accommodate the horses, and as there were available two buildings within a distance of some 50 or 60 feet, which are part of the works of the Canada Car and Foundry Company, one of those buildings was used for the accommodation of the men and the other for the horses. This year the winter fair building has been used, for the reason that no accommodation for horses was required, and it was well adapted as a barracks for the men. Furthermore, it was owned by the town of Amherst, and it was given rent free, with an understanding on the part of the town that it would be available for the uses of the Government until the war is over. The abandonment of the quarters in the buildings of the Canada Car and Foundry Company did not involve any loss; in fact, even with the additional cost of fitting up the winter fair building, the Government will be in pocket, for the reason that the 
extra insurance and the various incidental charges of watchmen and that sort of thing would make the continued occupation of the Car and Foundry Company's building far more expensive than to pull out the fittings, as was done, and transport them to Aldershot to be used for military purposes. Let me point out that while the cost of the equipment of quarters in the building of the Canada Car and
10 p.m. Foundry Company was something like $26,000, that cost included accommodation for one full regiment of infantry, a squadron of cavalry, and in addition, 750 horses; that the buildings that were fitted up this year-that is the winter fair buildings-were fitted up for the accommodation of one infantry regiment alone; and if my hon. friend will look at the returns which he has before him, he will observe that it cost more to fit up the buildings this year for the one regiment of infantry than it cost last year for the regiment of infantry, the squadron or cavalry, and the horses, combined. I do not know that I have covered all of the ground which has been gone over by my hon. friend, but I wish to do so. I do not wish to avoid any detail, and if there are any questions in connection with the matter which the hon. gentleman wishes to raise, I should be glad if he would do so.
The hon. member criticised the awarding of a contract for hay and fodder. I have only this to say with respect to that contract, that I was responsible for its having been awarded. It was given in the manner I have indicated, being one of the first awarded. I saw that it went to one of the most responsible and honourable farmers in the constituency, a man in whom I have entire confidence. My hon. friend criticised the prices, but he did not tell the committee that the Government did not buy a pound of hay, Let alone sqveral hundred tons, with the result that this farmer, on this contract, lost something over $1,000. I have been importuning the Militia Department for nearly a year asking them to compensate this man for his loss on the contract, and I believe that I have them convinced that he has a just claim and that he will be paid at least a portion of his loss. So far from having made any profit on the contract, he made a loss of the amount I

have mentioned. My hon. friend also says that one prominent Liberal was told that he could not get a contract because he was a Liberal. I would like to know who made the statement; I would like to have names.
I read it in the newspaper.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes,, but about threequarters of what you read in the papers was not true.
That may be.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
And the other quarter
was a very substantial loqking structure built out of a very delicate fabric; there was a very small modicum of substance in any of the statements which the hon. gentleman read from the newspaper. If the hon. gentleman has any ground for believing that anything is wrong in connection with the awarding of contracts, his . remedy is open and he can have it out in the Public Accounts Committee to his heart's content) and I for one, just as well as my hon. friend for Westmorland, will welcome the opportunity of seeing these various matters investigated.

My hon. friend has taken us very fully into his confidence, in regard to the awarding of contracts in Cumberland county. If it was a proper thing to give notice of my intention to bring up this matter, 1 offer my [DOT]'apologies for not doing so, because I certainly did not know that it .*.as customary on referring to a small matter like this to give any particular notice. 1 brought it up, not because I had the slightest feeling in regard to the matter. My hon. friend and myself have always been personally very warm friends, and I trust we may remain so. I brought this matter up because it had been brought to my attention, as I said at the outset, by a very reputable and responsible public journal in the countty of Westmorland, in New Brunswick. The editor of this , journal is, both financialy and in every way, responsible to answer for any charges that he makes in regard to public matters. I distinctly stated that I was taking my information from the newspaper that had published the statements and I was bringing it to the attention of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister for if it was true it was a disgrace and a shame that
the money had been so wasted by extravagance in the carrying on of the work in the adjoining county of Cumberland. I wish to -say to my hon. friend that if it was not true it should be cleared up because it was attracting a great deal of attention in that 'quarter and was -being used in a manner very detrimental to the Government as well as to recruiting in that portion of the country. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will assume that the hon. member wishes to be fair. I said that, following the custom of the Militia Department in the past, contracts over a year ago had been awarded. What is the date of the newspaper from which my hon. friend has read.

It is with reference to the

speechtext:
I have stated that for

That is what the hon. gentleman said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The first contract was

I will acceipt my hon.
friend's word that it was made on tender, but the only people who were allowed to tender were the political friends of the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes, in the first instance.

That is what I was talking about. That is the charge which is made

in this paper, that it was in the first instance. My hon. friend says that tenders were called for and that contracts were awarded, and he excuses himself on the ground that it had been the practice of the former Government to act in the same way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I said the practice of

The practice in the department, if my hon. friend wishes to play upon words. If he wants to hide behind the statement that it was the practice followed 'by the Militia Department under the previous Government, let me ask him if that is a sufficient excuse. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The effect of the hon. member's statement, as it would appear in Depress to-morrow, would be that the practice of this Government was not to award contracts by tender and contract or by the publication of tenders, but that it was the practice to award contracts under a system of political patronage, which is entirely and absolutely untrue.

I will come to that. I do not want to take the least advantage of my hon. friend, or to allow anything to go out to the public press that is not absolutely correct. Mr, RHODES: I did not say that I changed it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

You said so far as you
know.

He means that your
knowledge might go further.

Then in common parlance
would my hon. friend not say that his partner was a dispenser of patronage when he was not there? I want to be perfectly fair. My hon. friend's law partner.

Until very recently.

My hon. friend has not satisfied me, nor, I think, the committee,
as to whether or not this man, or some one else, up till very recently at least, looked after patronage matters.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Do not cover up this thing; let us get at the facts. What I have said is based on my knowledge of Cumberland County and upon information that I have. I have had business relations with Mr. Sterne. Surely my hon. friend would not attempt to make us believe that he had not some one in the county of Cumberland to look after the dispensing of patronage

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We- were discussing the
question of purchases by the Militia Department. I am consulting Mr. Sterne every day with respect to appointments in my constituency. I wired Mr. Sterne to know if he thought this man would be suitable for the position, and he wired back " yes." I know the man, I have known him for a number of years, but I do not know his religion or politics.

Does not that exactly prove what I .say, that Mr. Sterne is the dispenser of patronage and that he is referred to by my hon. friend whenever an appointment is made? My hon. friend applies to him in connection with the appointment of this man. He had to get Mr. Sterne's recommendation before he appointed him. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I believe so.

That being so, I want to congratulate my hon. friend upon having taken that course in regard to war expenditures, particularly because if there are any expenditures in regard to which no patronage should be -allowed they are the expenditures in connection with this war . My hon. friend apparently would like to have this committee believe that because there was no hay purchased, the statement I made was absolutely -incorrect. I told the committee, when I referred to it, th-at they expected to have

horses billeted there, and contracts for hay were let. I did not attempt to deceive the committee by saying that there was any hay supplied, because 'I knew better than that.
I knew there was no hay supplied. In fact, my hon. friend was being importuned to make up for the loss because some of his friends did not get an opportunity to supply hay and oats. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not admit that; I did not say anything with respect to the price at all.
Was not $21 a ton the price?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It may have been-I have not the figures before me-'but I did not mention the price.

Well, the statement was made that it was $21 -a ton and if my hon. friend, does not know, surely we may take it for granted that that was the price at which the hay was contracted for. My hon. friend knows as well as I do that at that time-$21 a ton was $3 or $4 more than hay was being purchased for.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not know anything of the kind.

Then I may inform my hon. friend that $21 a ton was $3 or $4 more than the highest price the farmers were being paid for hay at that time. He says that he had that contract let himself to his own political friends at $21 a ton with the expectation that a large quantity of hay would be used for billeting h'OTses and remounts at that place during that winter. The principle involved ig what I am talking about and what I am trying to impress upon the Prime Minister is that in the expenditure of this war vote he should see to it that no patronage is allowed to creep in or that any excessive prices, are allowed to friends of the Government when supplies are purchased. My hon. friend also claims that I have made these remarks because there is a prominent Liberal from Amherst here. That was the first intimation that I had that there was a prominent Liberal from Amherst here, and I shall be very glad to see him, hut his presence has nothing to do with my remarks upon this question, I simply brought the matter to the attention of my hon. friend in the most candid manner feeling that extravagance bad occurred in the past and hoping 
that it would not occur in the future. My hon. friend says that the cost of fitting up the Canada Car and Foundry building for troops was some *[DOT]$26,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: State the figures approximately.

That is approximately correct. There is a building that w.as fitted up for troops and for only five months at a cost of $26,000; it cost another large amount of money to demolish it and fit up a building somewhere else. When this building was fitted up for the billeting of soldiers during five months of the winter, why was it necessary to dismantle it and go to the expense of fitting up another place in the same town for the billeting of soldiers? If that is reasonable, if that is good business, then I admit that I do not know anything about what good business is. After this large expenditure had been incurred for fitting up and arranging the building I cannot understand why it was necessary to tear it down after one winter's use and go to expense in fitting up another place.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Probably the prevailing reason was that the building was not available for continuous use. It was being used this winter for the construction of cars, not to as large an extent as it was, but in part and it is being used now for that purpose.

If this building was only
going to be wanted for one winter it was hardly necessary, even though it gave to my hon. friend's company a chance to sup-/ply a certain amount of lumber, to fit it up. It does not seem to have been good business enterprise, even although the lumber was supplied by my hon. friend's company, to fit this building up when it was only going to be used for five months. My hon. friend asked me to bring this matter before the Public Accounts Committee. It is not necessary to bring it before the Public Accounts Committee because he admits the charges in regard to the letting of contracts and that is what this whole newspaper article and argument- are about. No word has been said about the letting of contracts during this past winter and I have not heard anything with regard to it? If he had pursued the course that he tells the committee he has pursueid, he would be able to tell us that contracts had gone to the lowest tenderer. If my hon. friend had pursued that course no fault could be found with him. But my hon. friend says that a commission went

down through the Maritime Provinces last summer, that invitations were held out to parties having charges to make against the Government, or any department of the Government, to go and make their charges, and they would be investigated.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
That is right.
*Mr. OOiPP: That may be true. But what better position should we be in to-day if that 'Commission that went through Nova Scotia had investigated these charges and taken evidence? We should not have known anything more aJbout it than we do to-day. We have no report from that Commission as to the charges they did investigate in Nova Scotia; we know nothing whatever about it. My hon. friend from Cumberland has admitted that the charges made by the Moncton Transcript are absolutely correct. While he admits he did wrong-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, I do not.

If it was not wrong at first it would not be wrong now. My hon. friend took great credit to himself just now that tenders had 'been called for in every instance, and contracts let to the lowest tenderer. If you read between the lines you could see that he was taking great credit/to himself for that, because it would have been discreditable to do the business in any other way. I repeat, the charges have been admitted by my hon. friend, and I trust that, now he has apparently resolved to do better in the future, his example will be followed by all the other members from the Maritime Provinces.

I intervene	in this discussion
with some	reluctance,	because I
have a very great question in my mind * as to whether this discussion should really be taking place. I think, Sir, there is room for grave doubt whether we are not losing our sense of proportion in the greatest crisis that has ever been passed through by this country, by this Empire, by the world, and by the world's prospects of the advance of civilization. I intervene from a strict sense of duty, and because I think it would be unfortunate that a vote of this magnitude in connection with a war of this magnitude, should pass without a note of clear support of the Government at this crisis, coming from this side of the House.
I come from a province where up to the
present moment we have recruited 2,656 more men than make our quota towards the
500,000	at which the Government is aiming. That is a fact of which, as an Albertan, I am reasonably proud, and that is a fact for which I find the explanation, if it is to be found, in this: that the people of Alberta are not so much concerned where the sugar is being got for the troops, as they are in getting the troops and beating the Germans.
I listened with very great care to the statement of my right bon. friend the Prime Minister from beginning to end. I listened to it calmly, and as I listened I was proud to be a citizen o.f Canada, and proud to he a citizen of Canada because of what the present Government of Canada has done in connection with this war. There were certain things which loomed up before my mind as I listened to that statement, and the first thing with which I was impressed was the magnitude of the burdens and the responsibilities which came upon the Government of a small portion of the British Empire with the swiftness and the suddenness that we know characterized the commencement of this war. It was my privilege, as it was my honour, at the beginning of the war, and as it has been more than once since, to express what was my clear convictions then, and what is equally my clear conviction now; that the head of this Government and the Government itself and the majority of its supporters were seized at once with the importance of the issues, and bent their whole energies to the task of contributing a proper quota on the part of Canada to the successful prosecution of the war. That was my conviction then and it is my conviction now. and I am clear in my own mind that history will record-whatever may be the petty political fortunes of party in this country at the next or any other election

I am confident that the impartial historian will record that my right hon. friend who leads the Government has from the day the war-cloud burst kept a single eye to the winning of the war, and has not been led aside or diverted from that purpose by any small motive or any small consideration whatsoever.
The next thing that loomed out in front of me as I listened to the statement of the Prime Minister was the point that was referred to by the right hon. gentleman himself, and that was the tremendous task which had fallen upon a.large and momentarily increasing number of the staff of the Militia Department, and of the loyalty

(Edmonton) I wish to ask a few questions in regard to matters more or less directly connected with the subject now before the committee, and I will do so later if this is a suitable occasion to secure information with regard to matters of detail.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There are a few matters about which inquiry is made, and I will speak very, briefly with regard to these and then take up what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) wants to know. If I am not able to give the information he requires, I shall have inquiry made, so that the information may be available at a later stage.

My intention was to ask questions with regard to matters of administration, but I will forego that for the moment. The hon. member for Red Deer has introduced a new note into this debate. Up to the present time, as I understood it, no question had come before the committee as to any lack of support to the Government in its proposals before the House. I understood that there was absolute unanimity in willingness to vote the money and support the Government. But there has been discussion in committee, as is right and proper, as to matters of detail. Some of these matters might foe of greater importance and some might be of lesser importance, but I submit that all this discussion was with a view to securing greater advantage and a greater efficiency in the proposals of the Government, in its administration and in its expenditure. If my hon. friend takes the position that because this country is at war the Government must be supported in everything, right or wrong, good or bad, and that that must be done with a view to securing success in the war, I can only say to him that in my humble judgment that is the wrong way to secure success. Success will never be achieved by that means.
Can my hon. friend quote a phrase from what I said that would indicate that as an opinion of mine-not a phrase?
My memory is not good for details, but I gathered from the enthusiastic applause with which his remarks were received that that was their import, to our friends on the other side at any rate.
I should say that the silence on your own side would indicate that.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Clark) said very specifically that he had not time to criticise or assist in criticism of the Government at this present time. He declared that the Government was doing the best that could be done, or if it was not, it was to be excused for not having done that very best. My appreciation of the position is this: while we recognize the stupendous responsibilities that have been placed upon the Government of the day by the outbreak of war; while we recognize that the conditions, call for every support that is possible to be given to the Government in the discharge of those responsibilities, the very fact of the greatness of the responsibilities that are on the shoulders of the Government lays the responsibility upon the shoulders of -members of the Opposition to take their proper part as critics of the action of the Government, and they cannot divest themselves of that responsibility by saying yea and amen to everything that is put before them by the Government. There has not been captious or partisan criticism of the Government during this debate. There has been no unworthy criticism of the Government or its administration. What might seem to be trivial matters may have been considered, and some important matters may have been considered, but I ask this committee, who is to say that a matter which tends to affect the mind of the people at this particular time is a trivial matter? Let it be small in material importance, if you will; if those who are discharging the responsibilities of government in this country are not dealing' fairly or squarely or honestly or with a sufficient sense of their own responsibilities, is that the way to win the war? Is that the way to get that unanimous support that we must have in order to win? That is not my appreciation of the situation. We on this side of the House are elected to this position for the 
purpose of criticising the Government. That is our business, the country looks to us to see that the actions of the Government that are open to criticism shall be criticised on the floor of this House, and we as members of the Opposition will be doing far less than our duty if we fail to make that criticism when it is called for by the circumstances. The civilization of the world is to-day in danger. It is in danger because it is being attacked by the greatest organization of military efficiency that the world ever saw. How is civilization to be protected? Are we to meet efficiency with inefficiency? Unless we meet efficiency with efficiency, civilization goes down; and we cannot have efficiency unless in this country of free government we have fair but free criticism. We look across the water and we see a Government in power in Great Britain relieved during a period of a year or more from the ordinary vicissitudes of parliamentary debate, of opposition, of criticism. It is not for us iat this distance to criticise what has been done over there, but I think no one will come to the conclusion that the experiment has been to the advantage of the Empire or the Allies or the cause of civilization. I say it would he deplorable for the part Canada is to play in this war if we in this country took such a position as has been taken over there. I do not suggest for a moment that I am here to criticise what has been done there. They have their special responsibilities, and we on this side are not in a position to say how best they may meet them. But the fact remains that the dispensing with political criticism in the Parliament of Great Britain has not resulted in success for the Allies; and we cannot expect that if we are to take the position that my hon. friend (Mr. Michael Clark) has suggested here to-night, we would have any better results. We have a duty to perform, and we must perform that duty. Our appreciation of the' matter is this: in the discharge of our responsibilities as critics of the Government of the day we are doing our part to win the war just as much as the Government is doing in discharging its responsibilities. I hope my hon. friend will pardon me if I do not agree with him, but my view is that if we took the position that he has outlined for himself, we would certainly not be doing what we should do to secure success; and that way failure lies.' Efficiency is what we want. Efficiency is what we must have. We need efficiency to the last limit, and we can only get it in the

administration of the country's affairs, as in any other line of life, by the friction that comes of mind against mind by criticism and discussion of important matters.
The Premier in giving to the House a statement the other day of the number of men enlisted and their location, spoke of the casualties and of the wastage. He said that the casualties amounted to something over 20,000 and the wastage to about- the same or a little more. What is the exact meaning of wastage?

speechtext: It would include all men who, for any reason whatever, are discharged from the service after having been once enlisted, for example, men who, upon a second examination, are not permitted to go to the front; men who are invalided from disease or any cause before going to the (front; .men dismissed from the service on account of misconduct or cri-me, deserters and minors.
