speechtext: The idea which the W7ar Office has in -min-d, -and which it supports by a memorandum, which was transmitted to us through the Colonial Office, is that giving the casualties with the numbers of the battalions gives certain information to the enemy which it is un- * desirable to afford.

' Of course, I am not responsible for the conduct' of the British

armies in the field, but I am one of the people of Canada who have some interest in the armies in the field, and I am going to say upon my responsibility as a member of tne House of Commons that I do not think that the advantage compensates at all for the disadvantage. Of course, we have to accept the situation as it is.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We hardly felt like taking the responsibility of declining to accept a very strong representation, which, as we understood, had behind it the support of the Commander-in-Ohief and the General Staff at the front.

In expressing my opinion I am exercising a privilege, which, I appreciate, could not very well be exercised 'by the Government. Iln connection with the publication. of the casualty lists there is another feature to which I wish to draw attention.. The list, as published, is a number of days, say three, four, or five days, or a week be hind the actual facts. The other day I received a telegram from a man in Edmonton giving the name of his son, who had been wounded, and wishing me to get particulars as to his condition. He had been wounded, I think, on the 8th of April, and it was not until at least a week after that date that the young man's name appeared in the casualty list, indicating that the casualty list does not represent the losses of the immediately preceding day, or, indeed, of any particular day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is quite true, so far as the immediately preceding day is concerned. But my hon, friend must remember that the information has to be picked up, in the first place, under the fire of the German batteries at the front, amid all the confusion and strain which are incessant under the conditions which prevail at the front. The identification number of the man must be obtained; sometimes he may have lost his life in a situation which renders it impossible to get near him at the moment. Delays are absolutely inevitable. After that has been done the information has to be transmitted to London, and then across the Atlantic. The code messages must be deciphered; the man's number must be compared with the records we have here, and a telegram must be sent to his immediate relatives. It must also be ascertained that the telegram has been delivered, and then, and not until then, 
can the information be made public in the press.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I can .conceive that the military authorities at the front might not regard it as a prudent course to indicate the precise number of casualties that had occurred in the Canadian forces on a particular day. I can easily conceive that they might take that in view. However, that may be, I do not think they ask us to pursue a different course from that pursued on the other side of the Atlantic. So far as I know, the method of making public the casualties is precisely the same there as here.

I am going to take the liberty at this- time, and on this occasion, to express the view of the Canadian people who are interested-I am taking the liberty of saying that it is the view of the Canadian people. The Canadian people are interested in these casualties more than anybody else, and I claim that they are entitled to be considered in regard to the matter of their publication. The impression on my mind is that these casualties are fed out, so to speak, judiciously -in the opinion of those in authority-with the view fhat they shall not alarm the public by giving too large numbers on any particular occasion. That is to say, those who at the moment have

authority in these matters do not, in their wisdom, think that they can trust the public with a knowledge of their losses from day to day. They are afraid to trust the public. They treat the people who are offering their fathers and brothers and sons as a sacrifice in the Empire's cause as if they were not to be trusted. They do not deal with them honestly and fairly and above board. They do not say: yes, on a certain day such and such a thing occurred, and such and such casualties were suffered. They say: we are in control; we are afraid to let you know, and we will only give out just as many casualties as we think ought to appear on a particular day. I am speaking on my responsibility as a member. I am not criticising this Government. But I say that that is not fair; it is not right, it is not good business. It is not the way to win the war for the Government, or for those who are in control of military affairs, to maintain an attituue of distrust towards tiie people upon whom they must aDSolutely depend, and who must absolutely trust them for success. If they do not trust the people, the people cannot trust them. If they do not trust the people to the extent of telling the truth in regard to that matter, which is so close to their hearts, the people cannot trust them in their administration of affairs. I go further, and say that, in my humble judgment, the dissemination of information by the military authorities has been used very much more to deceive and mislead the people of their own country, and to cover up their own incompetence, than to mislead the enemy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Is my hon.
friend referring to the action of the department here?

No, I do not know whether it is the department here or the department there. Whoever it is, they are not treating the people who are making the sacrifices with fair consideration; they are not giving them their confidence, and it is not being done for the good of the Empire; because everything that detracts from the confidence of the people in the conduct of military affairs certainly does not tend towards the people giving their support. There are many other matters that I wish to deal with, but as I understand the Prime Minister wishes to make a reply to what has been said, I will postpone what I have to say further to some other occasion.

I wish to congratulate my right hon. friend the Prime Minister upon having appointed officially General Lessard. The people of Quebec are very jealous of their heroes, and they are in that connection very conservative in a way. They are proud of them, whether in politics, in religion, in literature, in the arts or in military matters. General Lessard is one of them. Will my right hon. friend, who is a friend of the province of Quebec, listen to my candid advice? General Lessard has gone to the front to inspect officially troops, and no better man could have been selected; in fact, it was a surprise, and indeed a matter of regret, that his services should have been ignored since the beginning of the war. But, I did not rise to criticise. When his task on the other side is completed, I would ask my right hon. friend to give us back General Lessard in the province of Quebec, and I make bold to say that under General Lessard, Quebec will raise more battalions, because the province has confidence in his military efficiency, in his capacity, in his judgment. Fathers and mothers will be quite ready to confide their sons to the leadership of such a distinguished military officer.
I say this because there has been criticism in the press of the various provinces of Canada as regards recruiting in Quebec. I sincerely regret that there is not a happier feeling existing between the French-speaking population and the English-speaking population in Canada; I mean in the back concessions of the country. We have our own extremists, and my Englishspeaking friends have their own extremists. I am always reminded of the opening sentence in Lord Durham's report, which xuns as follows: "I came to Canada in the expectation of finding one country and one people; I found two countries and two peoples." Since the beginning of the war there has been, generally speaking, bad feeling as regards the attitude of the province of Quebec, and if I speak of that particular subject this evening it is because I think it is relevant to the issue, and because I wish to, if possible, clear the sky.
It has 'been stated that the French-Cana-dians were not enlisting as they should. Let me make on this subject a frank statement to the committee. There are surely people with heads on their shoulders who read the daily papers. Every morning since the famous battles of Langemarck and St. Julien, the roll of honour is published in

those daily papers, and I can find in it the names of the young English-speaking Canadians and of the young French-speaking Canadians who enlisted with the first contingent. In this morning's Le Canada among those in the casualty list I read the names of Paul Adrien Lambert, Lachine; Charles Richard, Montreal; Louis Savard, Quebec; Edouard Goulet, Trois-Rivieres; Joseph Mongeau, Sorel; Hormisdas Berthiaume, St. Eugene; Romulus Bourget, Montreal. If any one takes the trouble to scrutinize the list every day he will find that there is quite a galaxy of young men from my own province who on the battlefield are doing their duty to their country, to their King and to the Empire. Let me pay my respects to the British-born in Canada. They have done wonderfully well. They responded to the call as true Britons shoulu respond where-ever they may live. If I speak of the British-born in this way it is because in connection with the figures I intend to give the committee, I must make a distinction between the British-bosn, the Anglo-Canadians and the Franco-Canadians, in order to be fair and just to the people of my own native province who ,are ibeing accused in some parts of Canada of shirking their duty in this war. If my right hon. friend will give us General Lessard he will find that the habitants of Quebec will respond cheerfully. I have already invited my right hon. friend to visit the province of Quebec, but he could not accept the invitation on account of his sessional duties, but if my right hon. friend, who commands the respect of my province, as he commands the respect of the country, will come to Quebec with my right hon, friend who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), and with some of his ministers, we on this side of the House will join with him and we will make an appeal and thus swell the number of the existing French-Canadian battalions.
Coming back to the British-born: When the first contingent left Quebec, the figures were as follows: There are 33,000 soldiers gathered at Valcartier, and I say in passing that all credit is due the Government and the Department of Militia and Defence for the mustering of our yeomanry within such a short interval. Of the 33,000 soldiers who left Valcartier with the first contingent,
26,000	were British born.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Where does my hon. friend get his figures?

From Senators Mason's statement in the Senate the other day. Of

that 33,000,	2,500 were French-Canadians
who had responded to the call of duty and
4.500	Anglo-Canadians. I may be told that
2.500	is not a large number, but in speaking of recruiting in the province of Quebec, we must bear in mind certain facts, and I am glad that I am addressing myself this evening to leaders of the people from all provinces in Canada. First of all, Quebec is a self-sustaining province; she is the only province of the Dominion which does not receive any influx of immigration from abroad. Quebec receives no immigration from the British Isles, no immigration from the United States, no immigration from France, and practically no immigration from Belgium.

Where do all the Jews
and foreigners in the city of Montreal come from?

I was speaking of the
French-Canadians

not that I despise the Jews and foreigners in Montreal; for after a while they cease to be foreigners, and become naturalized and just as good Canadians as my hon. friend and myself. I am not speaking of what we call the foreign element, but of the native born French-Canadians. The increase in population of French Quebec, if my hon. friend prefers that description, is due solely to her birthrate, and we are rather proud of that. It is not so with the western provinces, or the great province of Ontario, to which flock nearly all British immigrants who come to Canada, In Ontario the trend is from the farms to the city: in Quebec, as all those who know the province will realize, the trend is in the opposite direction.
I hate to prove anything lby the law of averages, but what I am stating now I state in good faith, and in order to dispel any prejudices that may exist in the minds of the people. I think I shall be able to prove to the satisfaction o'f the committee and of the country at large that Quebec is not below her proper proportion of recruits at the present time. Do no't forget, that Quebec is above all things a rural province. We are being urged to increase production. Not later than two days ago I received a voluminous pamphlet UTging the people of Canada to go in for more production, and still more production; and only this afternoon we were told by the Prime Minister that production was an imperative, yes, even an Imperial duty. If he did not use that expression, .that is what I gathered from his remarks. The farming population in Quebec is primarily

needed on tlhe farms. Bear in mind the appeal that is now made from the platform and in the press, in the province of Ontario and other provinces, for more farm hands. In the province of Quebec, with the exception of the city of Montreal, the city of Quebec, the city of Sherbrooke, and to a certain extent, tlhe city of Three Rivers, our population is entirely rural.
What has the province of Quebec done in the way of recruiting since the beginning of the war? Let us face the facts without any prejudice, bearing in mind the situation as I have described it in good faith. I have stated that with the first contingent there were in round numbers
2,500	Freneh-iCanadians, and my right hon. friend will, I am sure, agree with what I aim now going to say. In many battalions, in the Maritime Provinces for instance, and in Northern Ontario, and the western provinces, there was quite a large sprinkling of FrencluCanadian volunteers. The other day Mr. M>ageau, tlhe local member for Sturgeon Falls, stated through the - press, that in a battalion organized in Northern Ontario at least 40 per cent were French-Canadian volunteers; and those who are familiar with conditions in my province and the facility with which the French-Canadian. absorbs other races, know that in many other regiments there are any number of Ross's, Scotts, Warrens, Camerons, Campbells, who would be very surprised if you addressed them in English, because their language is French. So that, in addition to the 2,500 French-tCanadians in the first contingent, at least 1,000 were sprinkled through the , various English speaking regiment's of Northern Ontario, amid eastern and western Canada. Since a year and a half ago we have had a recruiting! movement amongst the yeomanry of the province of Quebec, in which our public men are taking an interest. We have requested the Militia Department to favour the formation of French-Canadian units. I am glad to say the Militia Department gave a favourable answer to our request. I quite understand that there should be only one badge of nationality in this country-Canadian nationality. But look at what takes place in the Old Country. You have there the Irish Fusiliers, the Welsh Fusiliers, the gallant Scotch Grenadiers, and the English crack regiments. You cannot do away with these racial characteristics and affinities; they are deep-rooted, they are part of the soul of men of any
nationality. At the beginning of the war I urged very strongly upon the Minister of Militia that not only should we have French-Canadian units commanded by French-Canadian officers, but that the various corps should also have their own national uniforms. That, I confess, was a hobby of mine, and, perhaps, I was wrong. I advocated it to promote the cause of recruiting. We have at the present time in Quebec thirteen French-Canadian units or battalions. Some of them are at the front, others are in course of formation, and others are ready to start. I have said that
3,500	have already gone, and that is a modest figure. Then we have these other thirteen units of 1,100 per unit.
How many are filled up?
Nearly half of them are [DOT] filled up.
How are the others?

They are doing pretty well. I will give an instance. Yesterday I met Colonel de Salaberry. I may say, en passant, that I was instrumental in having Colonel de Salaberry brought from the front, where he had served with distinction. I .appealed to the Minister of Militia, and said: Here is Colonel de Sala/berry, the grandson of the hero of Chateauguay. He has served well and faithfully. Now we want a good name, we want a great name to induce our young men to follow the colours. The minister brought back Colonel de Salaberry, whom yesterday I met at church. Colonel de Salaberry has not been 'here more than four weeks, and he has already recruited 300 men. Three months ago. as the Prime Minister will remember, I asked him to give me a letter, which letter was read in Montreal at a public meeting to promote recruiting for the Desrosiers-Asselin regiment. Colonel Derosiers had been at the front. He was called back and started to form a regiment with Major As-selin. They had not one recruit three months ago, and to-day, I am pleased to inform the committee and the country, the Desrosiers-Asselin regiment is almost completed. Three months of reoruiting, three months of organization and work, has brought the battalion together. I think that within two months, when perfectly drilled and trained, the men will be anxious and eager to leave for the front. Now, let me give a list of our thirteen French Canadian units:

1.	22nd Battalion, under Colonel Gaudet, at the front.
2.	41st Battalion, Lieut.-Colonel Archam-bault, at the front.
3.	57th Battalion,Colonel Paquet.
4.	69th Battalion, Lieut.-Colonel Dan-sereau. Just left for the front.
5.	150th	Battalion,	Lieut.-Col.	Barre.6.	163rd	Battalion,	Lieut.-Col.	Desrosiers.7.	165th	Battalion,	Lieut.-Col.	Daigle.8.	167th	Battalion,	Colonel Readman-an
English name, mark well, but a French-Canadian.
9.	178th Battalion, Colonel Girouard.
10.	189th Battalion, Colonel Piuze.
11.	206th Battalion, Colonel Pagnuelo.
12.	230th Battalion, Colonel De Salaberry.
13.	233rd. Battalion, Colonel LepTohon.
Then there is the stationary hospital
under Lieut.-Col. Mignault, to which my hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) alluded to in very kind words this afternoon. Let me say, in passing, that speaking as one who has French blood in his veins, I thank the Prime Minister and the Canadian iGovem-ment for the noble gift they made the old Mother Country, in providing a Canadian hospital for those wounded in France. There is also the stationary hospital under Colonel Casgrain, and the one that left a few days ago under Colonel Beauchamp. There is also a corps of engineers which left several months ago under Major Janin. Unfortunately Major Janin perished with the Arabic.
Is that the whole list?
I have given the whole thirteen battalions.
I thought the hon. gentleman said thirty.
Assuming 3,500-a very low figure-as the number of those who went with the first contingent, then add these thirteen regiments-
Battalions.

I should have said
battalions. I am not a military man, although I have at the front a nephew who married a nice English-speaking girl from Ontario, and to whom I cabled " Good for you, you have settled the bi-lingual question." These thirteen battalions will number at least 14,000 men which, added to the number of those with the first contingent will make 17,500. I do not include the hospitals and the others I have already mentioned. But I say this to the Tight hon. Prime Minister and to my Englishspeaking friends on both sides of the

House: give us General Lessard and let the Prime Minister and his ministers and the public men on this side of the House make a proper appeal to the province of Quebec,det the press of Canada be fair and generous, and I make bold to say that the old province of Quebec will respond nobly to the call of duty, King and flag.
Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM: As we are all anxious that these resolutions should be reported to-night I trust the committee will bear with me for a few minutes. It is possible that I may not be here when the matter comes up in committee in the form of a Bill, and I would like to say a few words nown I do not think it requires any effort on my part, speaking in the absence of the leader of the Opposition, to reassure the Government, if that be necessary, that they have the hearty co-operation of every member in this House, no matter on what side he sits, in everything that is necessary to be done until victory finally comes to the cause which W'e all think is the noblest cause for which man ever contended. As to criticism, I think the Prime Minister invited criticism. Having been a member of a Government myself, let me quietly tell the members of the House who have not had that trouble on their hands, that although they may not think it, Governments like criticism. It is not an admission of ^weakness on the part of a Government to invite criticism. The Government would not dislike it if some of their own friends would criticise occasonally, and in this I sipeak from experience. 'Criticism enables a Government to stand off people of both political parties who ought to be stood off. Some criticisms may seem in Parliament to be of small importance, but nothing that tends to improve conditions can be called a small matter. I have taken considerable part in recruiting in my own weak way, and those things that we in Parliament regard as small are really the things that affect recruiting in the different localities. What is not a large matter to us sitting here to-night is mountain high in some localities when you appeal to the people on recruiting, or on behalf of patriotic founds. We must not however, lose sight of the magnitude of the war or forget the sense of proportions. Towering above all these things is the one great object we have in view, which is that Canada shall do her part, as she has been and is doing and will continue to do, until victory comes to the Empire. That is what we must keep in

view, and if I had time I would elaborate it, and say that even if we were not part of the British Empire, I would not feel that I was a good Canadian citizen doing my duty to my country, if I did not take some part in this fight for the betterment of world conditions.
The hon. member for Rouville has spoken of our fellow-citizen in the province of Quebec. Remember, we have many French Canadians in Ontario and throughout the West. I do not like to discuss these things, because we are Canadians, one and all, and in each doing his own duty, we will find that we have enough to do. Let us do our best in our own locality in the sphere in which we exert influence, and the results gained cannot but be good. If it be true that the recruiting in Quebec has not been what some people say it ought to have been, the men who have gone must have been of the real kind of stuff and worthy of the front ranks of any fight, because when we read the casualty lists we find French Canadian names dotted all through them. I say again that the men who have gone from the province of Quebec have not only brought lustre to their own province and to the land of their forefathers, but have brought credit and renown to the Dominion of Canada and to the British Empire as a whole. It would not be out of place for me to say as one not of French Canadian but of Irish descent, a word about the situation, as it may affect Canada, that has arisen in the land from which my forefathers came. In the present crisis John Redmond has proved himself a patriot of the right sort, a man who has won for himself greater distinction, if that be possible, than heretofore he enjoyed; a man who will have a bright page in the history of this Empire when it comes to be written in future years. He said recently, in condemning the outbreak in Dublin, that these foolish men were encouraged not only by Germans and German sympathizers, but by some misguided individuals on this continent. I think it will not be out of place for me to say, being of Irish descent, that there must be no mistake in the old land about the fact that in this case America does not include Canada. I know that I am justified in saying that from one end of Canada to the other the men who came from Ireland or whose fathers or grandfathers came from Ireland are true and loyal to the British flag. Ho people in the British Empire will condemn more strongly the outrages of misguided men in the city of Dublin, than will the Irishmen who have found a home in Canada.
I want to say this on behalf of the Militia Department. I myself have annoyed them terribly, although /I think the 'Government will not say that I have criticised their conduct unduly in the House. It is better for the Government, it is better for the Prime Minister that criticism should come, if it is of the right kind, and the Prime Minister was wise in inviting criticism. We are passing to-night a resolution for the raising of $250,000,000. Who will say that we have engaged in undue criticism if in one day we pass in this House a resolution giving the Government a credit for that enormous sum. There is no desire on t)he ipart of any person but to get what is best out of the money we are expending, so that satisfactory results may come from its expenditure. I say that I have annoyed the Militia Department incessantly about things that they may have thought small. I am afraid, with all due deference to some of the speakers to-night, that I have annoyed the Department with things as small as some people think the criticism was to-day. But what may seem small here is big in some localities. I sent my complaints to the Militia Department, whether the information I received was good, bad or indifferent. Being personally acquainted with the deputy minister, I have loaded him with a great deal of material that he may have thought useless and cumbersome, but I have always received most courteous treatment. When representatives of the people in Parliament take some pains in these matters, the people appreciate that the Government and its supporters and the .members of the Opposition are here to do the very best they can undeT these very serious conditions which confront us. Members sitting to our right and left, in front of us and behind us, are startled every time the telephone rings, jump every time a telegram is handed to them, are almost afraid to see an official of the Militia Department coming toward them, lest he have some bad news.
The situation has come home to us; members representing constituencies in this House have those dearest to them in the trenches, their lives hanging in the balance. Some have paid the highest tribute they could to their love of country, and it is with deep regret we have seen that a minister of the Crown has to mourn the loss 'of a dear son. It is a serious time, a serious situation. Whatever differences we

may have had, have sunk into- insignificance in the one great task we have in hand. I have, in going through the country endeavouring to do something in the way of assisting in recruiting, been asked a question that has been asked here to-day, and in a measure I answered it myself by my experience. I have been- asked: Why should, men without experience be given commissions as officers. There are in localities in Canada men who are not military men, men who have had no military training and who, on the field might be failures; but as men holding the respect of the communities in which they live and having the power of organization and the ability to attract men to them, they make better recruiting officers than any general you could send into a community. Many of these officers, I imagine, will never go the .front; I do not think they would be useful there, nor could they be trained in time to take charge of actual operations in the field. But until such time as the battalions are ready to be taken charge of for fighting purposes, these other men without training, are the very best men that can be secured to rally the recruits. I have several instances in my mind. In the city of Toronto, there is what they call the Sportsmen's Battalion, the officers of which have never had any military training, but they recruited that battalion with wonderful rapidity. That has occurred in several places*, and I have entirely altered my mind as to the necessity of a man having military training to get together a battalion, because many officers who have never had military training have shown themselves best able to get together the men, who can then be trained by experienced military officers.
This resolution is for a large amount of money, and while it is a sad duty to vote it, still that sadness must be tempered by the consideration that we are glad in Canada that we are able to vote it, and we are doubly glad that there is no dissenting voice to our voting it from one end of the country to the other. It is divided into several parts and "the defence and security of Canada," is the first. We have all read in the newspapers lately items which give a certain serious'aspect to that section. We have read recently of a plot unearthed in the city of New York for the destruction of the Welland canal and for other depredations in Canada. Money is
12 midnight, necessary for the defence of Canada in Canada. Even those, of whom there are very few, who still

insist that they should not go outside of Canada to serve the country, might possibly be put to work to do all this Canadian duty. We might take them on their own ground and put them to work defending Canada under this section.

They would not do
much good.
I should not like to say that.	.
You have to furnish the foe first.

Let not my hon. friend be so sure. As I was remarking, a plot was exposed in the city of New York, which if carried out, would have done an immense amount of damage not only to Canada but to the Empire. Perhaps the hon. member has read also a confession by a man in New York who said there was another plot to gather together a certain number of men near the Canadian border and rush them across. They could not have accomplished anything; they could have been taken care of if they had come across the line, and I have very grave doubts if they would have been allowed to cross. It is necessary that certain money should be devoted actually tc the defence of Canada in Canada, and I was making the suggestion that if it be necessary, the very few men in certain parts of Canada who insist that they are ready to fight but would not go outside of Canada to fight, should be utilized for that service.

With Choquette for
leader.

This resolution also provides " for the conduct of naval or military operations in and beyond Canada," which includes, of course, all the operations in which we are engaged, and which are of mighty import. The vote also provides for: " Promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risks or otherwise." This is not the most unimportant section of the resolution because if the trade or the industry of Canada in its various parts were to fall down, we might become a burden to the Motherland and the Allies, instead of an aid to them because, on the continuance of our trade and industry, as far as we possibly can continue it, rests our financial progress, and without that financial stability we might be a burden instead of an aid. Money expended along those lines is second in importance only to the money spent in buy-

ing munitions and paying for the men at the front. The resolution also provides money for:	" The carrying out of any
measures deemed necessary or advisable by the Governor in Council in consequence of the existence of a state of war." This section is one of some considerable importance. Then the resolution says:
Payments made for ttoe said purposes during the fiscal years ending respectively the thirty-first day of March, nineteen hundred and fifteen and the thirty-first of March, nineteen hundred and sixteen, in excess of the amounts authorized by the War Appropriation Act, 1914, and the War Appropriation Act, 1915.
At the beginning, of course, no person had any idea that the war was going to be of such magnitude or that the expenditure was going to be of such huge proportions, but now, we are prepared to accept almost anything. This clause must mean that the Government lias found itself obliged to expend a good deal of money, by Governor General's warrant I presume, in excess of the .amount provided in 1914-1915.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There have been no Governor General's warrants.
The money was expended in excess of the vote.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes. At least
liabilities have been incurred. I think they came to about $10,000,000 more than the amount provided in 1914-15 and to about $50,000,000 more than the amount provided in 1915 and 1916, the reason in the latter case being, of course, that the establishment was increased very much beyond the number estimated for when we voted the $100,000,000 last year.

I was not finding fault
with the money being expended; I was referring to the method in which I supposed it had been expended, and I was going to say that I hope that in the future- and I hope that the future will be very much restricted-the vote we are making now will be fully ample to meet the requirements without being over-expended. Of course if the necessity arises, Parliament will uphold the Government in any expenditure necessary, but it will be wise to make the amount as large as we think will be needed so that the Government may not be put in the position of over-expending the appropriation. These are things that struck me as I was reading the resolution. No matter what we may think, this is a very important resolution. It involves an enor-ous amount of money, and while we are
anxious to put it through and expect to put it through in a very little while, it is wise that we should understand it and understand what is expected to be done, always keeping in mind that it is efficiency we are after and not carping criticism. I might ask the Prime Minister whether, when the Bill is in committee, he will be able to give us information as to the probable expenditures under the various head? in the resolution, or whether the Bill founded on the resolution will be subdivided in that way. I am not asking for that information to-night, because it would involve too much detail, but when the committee comes- to deal with (he Bill founded on this resolution I presume that questions will be asked, and the Government shomd be in -a position to give us an idea of vs hat is likely to be the subdivision or expenditures for the coming year.
Let me say, in conclusion, that no matter what party they may belong to

I do not care from what country their fathers or grandfathers came, or how long they have been here; no matter what the differences of opinion may be, or what criticism may be made of what the Government has done, or has not done, let all the people of this country understand; let the people of the Empire fully understand, as they do; let the Allies understand, and, above all, let our enemies understand that the Canadian people are as one behind the Government until this war is won and victory crowns the cause to which we are all so devotedly attached.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I appreciate very much what has been said by my hon. friend who has just addressed the committee, and who has given evidence that he understands the very great responsibilities which have devolved upon the Government in the conduct of this war. Responsibilities have come upon us, especially during the past year, with the vastly increased establishment of the military forces, which no one of us could have anticipated in August, 1914. Not only has the magnitude of the war proved greater than we supposed at that time, but its probable duration will also be much longer than any of us then imagined. I am also- very grateful to the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) for his appreciation of those responsibilities, and for his tribute to the purpose of the Government in what it has done towards making our part in this war effective. Probably no one who has not been brought

closely in touch -with those responsibilities can adequately appreciate what they have been. Therefore, a word from any hon. member of this House testifying to his understanding of what the burdens of Government have been during the past eighteen or twenty months is- very acceptable to those who have had to bear the weight of those responsibilities.
While I do not in the least suggest that the discussion has been too long-I would not have been surprised if it had lasted more than one day upon the resolution	itself-nevertheless, some of the
matters which have been dealt with were of a rather trivial nature, as has been observed, although they may loom very large, as the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said, in the immediate communities which they concern. So far as the responsibilities of the Government are concerned, I hope it will be understood, not only by the members of this House, but by the country, that the various transactions and affairs carried on through an enormous territory in this country are in many cases absolutely beyond the direct control of any member of Gio Government, or, for- that matter, of any departmental officer. Naturally such traos-actions cannot be dealt with by a wholly centralized administration in a country which extends nearly 4,000 miles from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and which is composed of a great many scattered communities.
In the first instance, I should like to refer to the question of patronage, whicn has been discussed by a good many hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. Let me affirm to the members of this committee, and to the country, that, so far as I am concerned, and so far as the Minister of Militia is concerned-he has had mostly to do with them-there has been absolutely no desire or intention on the part of the Government to. deal with these matters from any party political standpoint. In the early months of the war the question of contracts was brought to my attention by an hon. gentleman who owns allegiance to the party which is represented on the other side of the House, and I told him at that time that it was not seemly or desirable, whatever the practice might be in ordinary conditions, that such matters should be dealt with from a party political standpoint. I am in a position also to affirm, on behalf of the Minister of Militia, that that was precisely his own view. Indeed, on many occasions, on countless occasions, I

might say, during the past 18 or 20 months the reproach has been made to me personally, and it has been made with regard to the Minister of Militia, that party considerations had been absolutely put aside, and that the conduct of this war by the Government had been of such a character as to discourage some members of the Conservative party. These reproaches have even been carried to the extent of suggesting that military officers who had been appointed by the Minister of Militia and Defence were using the positions, which he had entrusted to them, for the purpose of injuring or discrediting the Conservative party. I have always said in reply to such representations that these officers had been selected for the reason that they were efficient, and because the Minister of Militia and Defence believed them to be the best men for the particular positions entrusted to them, and that I was not disposed, nor was the Minister of Militia disposed, to attach importance to representations of that kind. It is possible that in a number of localities persons affiliated with the Conservative party may have endeavoured to make use of patronage in regard to some of the matters complained of, but, so fab as any information which has come to me is concerned. I believe that the hon. gentlemen who have put forward those views in this comjnittee have been rather misled in the instances referred to, or that the cases have been very much exaggerated.
My hon. friend from Regina (Mr. Martin) referred to recruiting in small communities, and he doubted the expediency or value of that system which has been pursued during the past winter by the Minister of Militia and Defence. The minister discussed with me and with his other colleagues the method before it was put into operation, and it was his idea that keeping men a certain number of months in the community in which they were recruited would accomplish two purposes. In the first place, they would be under the eye of their immediate relatives, under the eye of the mothers and the fathers of the boys during the early months of their training. Their parents and immediate relatives would 'know the associations into which they were brought and would probably have greater confidence in sending them forward to camps at a later date if the early preliminary training took place in the communities where these young men lived. In the second place, he had in mind,

whether rightly or wrongly, that such training for a few months would be equally as valuable as it would have been if the method suggested by the hon. member for Regina had been pursued. As an illustration of that, may I point out to my hon. frind from Regina-whose remarks were put forward in a very reasonable way, and whose criticism, if it can be called criticism, was of a character that the Government will always welcome-that I see every day from my office window in the eastern block, men being trained upon the lawn of Parliament Hill and I see them being trained in squads of about eight. I have seen that going on day after day and for a time I wondered why it was so done. But I think I appreciate the reason for it, namely, that the first training which the soldier must receive is what is called squad drill and that can go on equally well in the community where a few men are recruited as in larger camps.
With regard to the criticism that has been made of the medical inspection, I have sought information from the Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence and he has informed me that our inspection in Canada is equally as strict as that in the United Kingdom. It may be that too much zeal on the part of recruiting officers has led to some influence being brought to bear on the medical men who examine these recruits; I will neither affirm nor deny that because I do not know. I understand, however, from the deputy minister that after these men are sent to camp, as they all will be sent to camp, a further medical examination takes place, and then very possibly some of the men who have been accepted by the local medical officers may be weeded out. It would be difficult to devise a method by which incidents of that kind would be entirely avoided. We have to select the medical men in different parts of the country. There has been some suggestion that they are selected on account of their political - affiliations. I venture to 'think that that cannot possibly be correct and I will give an illustration in my own constituency. In many cases, as I know, in Kova Scotia men are selected not by the Department of Militia and Defence but by the local recruiting associations. There was a gentleman in my own constituency, a man honoured by those who are hie friends politically and by those who are opposed to him, a man who has been in practice
for forty years or 'more in the locality in which he resides. There is also in the same locality a young man, a member of an old and well known family in that particular district, who lhas been in practice only two or three years, whose family has been recognized as the champions and leaders of Liberalism in that district for a great many years in the past. When it became necessary during the past year to select a medical officer for the examination of recruits in that district, the man selected was not the physician who had been practicing for forty years and who was honoured and respected by all and who happened to 'be a Conservative, but. the young man of two, three, or four years' standing who happened to belong to about the strongest Liberal family in the district. I should think that 'an illustration of that kind would convince hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House that the selection of medical officers has not been conducted in so far as the Militia Department is concerned, with any regard for political affiliations.
Then the statement has been made, that in some cases .a sufficient sense of responsibility has not impressed itself upon the officers commanding regiments or engaged in recruiting regiments. My hon. friend from Regina gave a reference to the case of Private Robert Darragh whose family, most unfortunately, were not made acquainted with news of his illness. I shall have that matter inquired into. As ,far as commanding officers of regiments are concerned, when well founded representations are made to the department that any officer is not discharging his duties with competence an inquiry is made by the Adjutant General. An hon. member on the other side .of the House within the past week wrote me a letter representing that a certain commanding officer was not filling the bill, ii I may use that expression, and that the particular regiment which he was recruiting would not be effectively organized or .properly trained unless some change were made. The course which I took is the one which, I believe, has been taken in all such cases by the department. The matter was referred to the Adjutant General to whose branch such matters naturally appertain, and he was instructed to send a special officer for the purpose of inquiring into the organization and probable efficiency of that battalion if it should continue under the command of that officer. The complexity of these matters that daily

present themselves to the officers of the Militia Department, and to the minister whoever he may be who is entrusted for the time being with the administration of the department, is very great indeed and probably beyond the conception of those who have not been brought personally and closely in touch with it.
My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) referred to some matters. I was rather surprised to. hear him express the view that I had ibeem taking undue credit to the Government, or to the department, with respect to what has been accomplished in this country. It has been my duty on a great many public occasions

I was not speaking
of the personal attitude of my right hon. friend because I did not accuse him of having made that statement, but I was referring generally to the claim that was made to the effect that the way we had responded to the demands of the war was a matter of wonder. I said that it was not a matter of wonder.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is another matter and I will come to it in a moment. It has been my duty on many different-occasions to point out, as I am glad to do now, that without the splendid spirit of the Canadian people, and the equally splendid support that they gave to the Government, it would not have been possible for any Administration to accomplish all that has been done in the past twenty months. Let there be absolutely no doubt about that. My observations were made rather for the purpose of impressing on the members of the committee, and upon the people of the copntry, the very great magnitude of the task that had been undertaken with the support of the Canadian people, and to express the belief that that task had been discharged in a manner fairly creditable to this Dominion and to its people. In regard to the number of men who have been enlisted, my observation was to the effect that not one of us would probably have believed in August, 1914, that within eighteen or twenty months 310,000 or 320,000 men would have rallied to the colours of this country, or that there would have been occasion for them to do so. It is all very well for us to-day, with all this accomplished by the Canadian people, to say we had no doubt upon the subject; but I venture to think that if we had looked forward in August, 1914, to the enlistment of 310,000 or 380,000 Canadians within the period that has intervened, we could hardly have believed that

it would have been accomplished with the expedition and efficiency which' we have witnessed.
My hon. friend also alluded to a supposed lack of enthusiasm because the militia units did not go forward as such. I have not found any lack of enthusiasm by reason of that or by reason of anything else. The mere fact that more than 102,000 men have rallied to the colours in the first three and a half months of this year indicates that there is no lack of enthusiasm in any part of this country; and as far as militia units -are concerned, there has been no reason why any militia regiment should not organize a regiment for overseas service. That has been done in several cases. It has been done, I am informed, by the 89th Rimouski Regiment and by the 65th Regiment of Montreal. The Grenadier Guards of Montreal, the 5th Royal Highlanders, the Victoria Rifles, the 48th Highlanders, the Mississagua Horse, the Queen's Own, the 10th Royal Grenadiers, the 90th Battalion of Winnipeg, the 55th Irish Rangers and other militia regiments have raised or are raising overseas' battalions with the parent regiment.
My hon. friend from Pictou also alludes to the work of a gentlemen who bears my own name, Colonel Borden, and I entirely agree in the appreciation that he has expressed of Col. Borden's work. He seemed to have some apprehension about the Highland Brigade. Let me tell him that those apprehensions are entirely groundless. The only question about the Highland Brigade and the 85th Regiment is this:	The 85th
Regiment was organized by Col. Borden, and is now fairly well trained and practically ready to go to the front. The only question to be determined is whether, inasmuch as the 85th Regiment under the command of Colonel Borden was really ready to go to the front and had been organized for - a considerable time, and having regard to the further fact that if the regiment was retained in Nova Scotia it would be very useful, not so much in the organization, but in the training of three other regiments which had been recruited there-the question is whether, having regard to these considerations, it would be better in the public interests for the 85th Regiment to go immediately to the front, oi to remain in Nova Scotia, going to Aider-shot or some other central point, and assist in training the new regiments which had really been raised through the efforts of Col. Borden in co-relation with the 85th, which he commands. The Chief of the

General Staff has been consulted about that, and I understand that Col. Borden himself has been sent for, and his opinion will be considered before any decision is arrived at.
My hon. friend referred to recruiting officers, and their inability to pay for a band. I really do not know anything about details of that kind. I do not suppose it would be proper to pay for a band unless there was some authorization for it from the Department of Militia and Defence. Recruiting has been carried on in many parts of the country by voluntary effort, and the Government is most profoundly grateful, and I think the people also ought to be profoundly grateful, to the men who, night and day, have been devoting their energies to this good work. It has been done to a very great extent in a voluntary way, and possibly it may have occurred that some of these voluntary associations have not been able to give an undertaking that the Department of Militia and Defence would pay certain expenses. All that, however, simply shows due regard for the public interests, to the end that public money shall not be expended except under adequate sanction
The hon. member for Pictou speaks of cold water being thrown on idealism by reason of the improper distribution of contracts for supplies. I do nut quite agree that the idealism of the people of this country is influenced by considerations of that kind. He speaks of some gentleman in Cape Breton having undertaken to bring the affairs of the Hospital Commission into a question of patronage.
No. The question was whether or not the Government was going to take a certain hospital, in which event he was going to prepare a list of employees whom he would recommend.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All these hospitals are regulated by a commission of gentlemen who have been appointed without regard to their political affiliations, and if there is any gentleman in Cape Breton or elsewhere who imagines that the Hospitals Commission is administering its affairs with a view to political patronage, all I can say is that that gentleman will find himself very thoroughly mistaken in the end.
I am not complaining about the Hospitals Commission.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With regard to the obtaining of commissions through favoritism, my experience of these matters has been that the Minister of Militia and Defence has sought to get efficiency, and has been guided by that consideration alone.
One- hon. gentleman opposite, I am not quite sure who it was, indicated that the Government might be subject to criticism whichever course was pursued. For example, if a Conservative was appointed to a particular commission, the allegation would be made that it was done through favouritism, and if a Liberal had been selected for the command, the allegation would be put forward that the commission was offered for the purpose of getting the man out of the way, and clearing the political atmosphere.
With regard to machine guns, about which my hon. friend from Pictou has made some inquiry, I do not understand that there was such an appeal made by the Government as he suggests. Let me state what the situation was. The Government of the province of Ontario, for example desired to make some contribution to the war through the Federal Government. They suggested and desired machine guns, and we accepted their proposal in the same spirit in which it was put forward. The /matter was fully explained to the public in a letter which I wrote to the Government of Ontario, and which I believe was made public by that Government at the last session of the legislature. A gentleman, a splendid patriotic citizen of this country, who had lost a very near relative in this war, came to the Government nearly a year ago and desired to make a contribution of $100,000 as a memorial, so to speak, of the sacrifice which his brother had made in giving up his life in this war. He was especially desirous that that sum should be utilized by this Government in the purchase of machine guns, and if the regulations of the War .Office would permit it, that those guns might be added to the ordinary establishment of regiments in the British service for our Canadian forces when they went to the front.
Was that Mr. James Car-ruthers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, it was Mr. Huntley Drummond, of Montreal. We assented also to>
that. Then the matter was taken up in the press, and appeals were made. At that particular time a great deal was said in the press as to the vast importance of machine guns at the front. The Government had not -been idle in the meantime. I remember, I think it was in October, 1914, when I was attending to the affairs of the Department of Militia and Defence for about a week, it was represented to me that unless a certain proposal that

was made to us with regard to the - provision of machine guns was accepted at once, we might lose them altogether. The number of guns in question was 250. I directed that the guns should be ordered at once, and they were ordered the same day the matter was brought to my attention. Further orders were given during the autumn and winter, and very considerable orders during the spring and summer of 1915. The Government had in mind the necessity of machine guns throughout. But when this campaign was made by the press in various parts of the country, patriotic people all over Canada were naturally very much interested and enormous sums of money were subscribed and very large amounts paid in. If I remember well the total amount otf subscriptions paid in was nearly $800,000. When I returned from Great Britain the matter was brought to my attention and I made a public announcement in the city of St. John as to what the desire of the .Government was. I have not the words before me, but I made it clear that so far as the provision of machine guns was concerned, that should be defrayed from the public treasury, and I expressed the hope that those desirous of giving of their means for patriotic purposes would contribute rather to the Patriotic Fund, the Canadian War Contingents Association, the Red Cross Fund and other movements of that kind. I found it necessary to make three or four public statements before the movement came to -a standstill. Then the question was, what should be done with the money that had been paid in? After very careful consideration we arrived at-the conclusion that it would not be desirable, or even possible, to repay those sums. In a few cases request was made of the Government that sums contributed should be repaid. In all such cases the same answer was given and the reasons explained why, under the circumstances, the Government thought it undesirable to begin repayment of these sums. One reason was that a portion of the money had been applied to the purpose for which it was given, apd we did not see that it would be useful or desirable to entertain any request for repayment.
My hon. friend from Pictou has also spoken of the commandeering of ships, and with a great deal of what he has said I desire to express my concurrence. I can assure him that this Government has not been behind hand in placing before the Government of the United Kingdom all the

considerations he has expressed, and in several instances at least we have induced the British Government to reconsider their determination to commandeer vessels engaged in the local trade of Canada. For very good reasons we took that stand. It is quite impossible for a committee of the Admiralty in 'London, upon which the Government or the people of Canada have no representative, to be thoroughly aware of the local conditions in this country, to be thoroughly aware of the interests of our people and their dependence upon water communication. All this has been put forward in very cogent terms, and on a very great number of occasions during the past four or five months that very subject has been the cause of urgent communication from the Government of 'Canada to that of the United Kingdom.
I join my hon. friend from Pictou in his tribute to the women of Canada for their splendid spirit of devotion and selfsacrifice in this war.
The hon. member referred also to recruiting for the naval service. I regret that I am not able to give information on that subject, but the Minister of the Naval Service, no doubt, will do so.
The hon. member was inclined to criticise the efforts put forth by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Finance to impress upon the people the importance of production and the necessity for saving. I do not think that an admonition of that kind is out of place, notwithstanding the view of my hon. friend to the contrary. I recollect being very much impressed by a remark made to me by a representative sent by the Government of Denmark to this country a few years ago, I met him for a few moments on Parliament Hill, and, in the course of a short discussion, I asked him: What is it that has impressed you most during your visit to this country up to the present moment? He answered:	If I may be perfectly frank
with you, the thing that has most impressed. me in this country during my visit is the awful waste that goes on in Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific." I think that increased production, the desirability of saving and the elimination of waste ought to be impressed upon the people of Canada during this war, and in my judgment the Department of Finance and .the Department of Agriculture have made no mistake in the movement for that purpose which they have initiated.

So far as cruel and unusual punishments are concerned, I entirely agree in condemnation of such methods. The Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence informs me that there is no warrant for them in the militia regulations. Every necessary investigation will be made-an investigation is being made at the present time,-and if it is found that the allegations made in this House with regard to this matter are well-founded, then the necessary action must of course follow.
My hon. friend from Kings, P. E. I. (Mr. Hughes) brought up matters with which I shall not trouble the House to any great extent, but I desire to say a word or two about some of them. As to powder milk, I am informed that the analysis to which exception is taken was made by the Dominion Analyst, and the department thought themselves entitled to rely upon it; also that the ration of which powder milk formed a part was determined by the Army Service Corps, and that tenders were called for in the usual course.
With regard to the advertisement of the Military College, he said that a newspaper somewhere in his province had not been permitted to publish it. The Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence informs me that the publication was restricted to a few papers, and that many Conservative newspapers have applied for permission to publish it and have been refused.
The hon. member says that " 600 canned Canadian officers "-to use his expression embodying some wild misinformation of which he has become possessed-are to be found in Great Britain at the present time. I am informed that a certain number of officers in Great Britain are what is called " supernumeries," but all are attached to some unit and all are employed.
Some hon. member on the other side, I think it was the hon. member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mi. J. J. Hughes) criticised members of this House who have put on uniform in the endeavour to do their duty as loyal, patriotic sons of this country. My hon. friend is sufficiently answered by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), who points' out that, even where men do not possess the military knowledge and experience which would enable them to go to the front, or even where they are beyond military age and could not face the physical endurance required of them if they should go to the front, nevertheless they can give real and valuable service to this country by devoting their energies in the communities where
they reside to promoting the enlistment of battalions which will go to the front. It seems to me that such efforts are not to be condemned, but are to be commended.
My hon. friend from Westmorland (Mr. Copp) spoke of many matters as to which answer has already been made by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes.) I will not pause to deal further with them. There was no wish or sanction on the part of the Government for any departure from well Tecognized and proper methods of administration in the county of Cumberland or elsewhere.
My hon. friend the member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) spoke of General Lessard having been ignored since the outbreak of this war. I must take exception to that statement, because General Lessard has been engaged in the discharge of exceedingly important duties. I do not believe that any man at the front has had responsibilities that are more important or that have been discharged more adequately than those assumed by General Lessard in his position as Inspector General. I know of his work in the province of Ontario, and I believe that he has rendered most valuable service to Canada and the Empire in the discharge of his highly important duties as Inspector General. The hon. gentleman has spoken of the assistance which General Lessard could render to the cause of recruiting in the province of Quebec; I should be very glad to take all that into consideration. I pay a tribute also to the gallant and loyal citizens of French origin from the province of Quebec who have gone to the front and who have in very many cases notably distinguished themselves. I paid the same tribute to them when I had the privilege of being in France and Belgium last summer. I had the honour on that occasion of congratulating some of them upon the fine service which they had rendered to this Dominion and the whole Empire.
My hon. friend the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) spoke of certain matters as to which I gave him answer at the moment, except in one respect. He suggested, indeed, he asserted, that the lists of casualties were being dealt with by some authorities-I am not quite sure whom he intended-not with the view of giving information to the public as it ought to be given at the earliest possible moment, but with the view of political expediency and in . order to cover up the shortcomings of those who are responsible for the conduct of this war. I desire sc far as this Government is



concerned to repudiate in the strongest terms consistent with Parliamentary usage any such statement as that. I am informed and I believe that the casualties are published in this country as speedily ^as possible consistently with the considerations to which I alluded when answering the hon. member for Edmonton. It is necessary in the first place that the next of kin so far as they are known shall be notified. The telegrams are decoded, the men are identified, all the detail that is necessary is dealt with, and after all that has been done the casualties are published at the earliest possible moment. So much is this the case that the staff of the Department of Militia and Defence which is charged with this duty remains at work until four or five o'clock in the morning whenever these casualty lists come in. The idea is, to give notice to the immediate relatives of those who are killed or wounded, and when it is ascertained that that advice has been given to the immediate relatives, not a moment's time is lost in making the casualties public.
I do not know that there is anything further with which I need trouble the committee at the moment. In conclusion, 1 hope hon. gentlemen on both sides and the people of the country will at least give those responsible for the administration of public affairs, under these circumstances of great strain and urgency, the credit of *believing that they are inspired by a fixed resolve to do their duty. 1S0 far as I am concerned and so far as my colleagues are concerned, we have devoted ourselves to the great common purpose, which is of the highest possible import not only to this country but to the Empire and to the world, with all the energy that in us lies.
Resolutions reported and concurred in.
On motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 143.55 a.m., Tuesday.
Tuesday, May 2, 1916.
